translations.text: Discourse of Basil, chapter one. [?] that heavy thing. For this reason, when we move it upward, it grows heavy on us toward the earth; and when we move [fire] downward, we force what belongs to fire to be drawn down below. And the drawing of material things toward what is opposed to them is the cause of their dissolution, for what is forced is outside nature.
And what is outside nature, through its own opposition, quickly comes undone from its established state, and returns again to that from which it was established.

Compelled by this, the wise men of the nations rejected what those first ones had said, and they proposed the nature of a fifth body to account for the heaven and the stars that are in it. Then another of those who had gone astray [?] his own argument: he opposed them, refuted what they had said and established his own argument. If we were to report it, we would be on a level with them in [?] inconstancy. Instead, let us leave them alone and let them refute what each other has said. Let us accept what Moses said about the existence of the heaven [?] here: "God created heaven and earth." Let us glorify the skilled Craftsman, who created with wisdom, and let us understand the Beautiful One from the beauty of what is seen. From [?] these perceptible and bounded bodies, let me consider the Infinite One, who is greater than [?] and higher than thoughts about the greatness of his [?power].

For even if we cannot understand the knowledge of [?] created things, the things that are beneath our [?] are so wonderful that even a wakeful mind [?] [?] to investigate the least of visible [?] things and to give glory to its Creator, who [?] forever and ever. Amen.

Discourse of the same, chapter two. Yesterday we touched on a few words and found a depth of understanding, a hiddenness, so that we lost hope concerning what remains. If the portico of the sanctuary is like this, and before the gates of the sanctuary it is so beautiful and graceful, and by its great beauty it enlightens the eyes of our mind, what then must the Holy of Holies be? And who is able to dare to approach that inaccessible place? And who may look upon those hidden things? For its face is terrible to look upon, and its word is hard to understand and hard to interpret. But since the reward of the righteous Judge is prepared for those who wish to do what is [required?], let it not seem to you [?] to investigate. For although we fall short of what is worthy, yet when we do not reason apart from the mind of the Scriptures, with the help of the Holy Spirit, we may be made contemptible, but we shall not be condemned, and with the help of grace we shall find some small thing.

"And the earth was invisible and unprepared." How is it, since both are equal in having been created, that is, heaven and earth, that heaven was made complete, while the earth was not yet prepared? What then is its unpreparedness, and what [?]? For the preparedness of the earth is its building up, which consists of: the sprouting of many plants, the appearing of tall trees, fruit-bearing and unfruitful, the many colors of flowers, and the fragrance [?] of others also, which were to come up by the will of God, so that they might adorn the earth, their mother,
And since [?] of them, it was called 'unprepared.'

And in this way we would speak concerning heaven [?], that it was unprepared [?], and the will [?] adorned it to the measure of what was needed, and made an oar or spade for sailors and for tillers of the land, and a spear-shaft for soldiers.
But when God, first of all visible things, willed and resolved to make the things that were not, and how this world should be, within his own thought he created matter together with its adornment.
And he assigned to heaven the nature that befitted it, and to the form of the earth the substance that resembled it.
And he created fire and water and air as he wished; and he made them in themselves, as befits each of them within its own boundary.
And the whole world, which consists of dissimilar parts, he joined and made firm by one communion, by an ineffable bond of blending,
so that even those things that are separate from one another in place became blended together by love.

And now let them fall silent from their vain words, and let them not compare the weakness of their reasonings with that power which is beyond the reach of human minds and cannot be uttered in their words!
"God created heaven and earth." He did not create some [?] part of each of them. He created the whole heaven and the whole earth, [?] made together with their form.
He does not merely receive the forms. He is the creator of the nature itself.
Otherwise, answer us this: how was the power of God blended [?] with the passible nature of matter, while one of these is a receiver, lacking its own form,
and the other has the knowledge of forms without matter, so that each of them might fill up the deficiency of its neighbor;
for is it the Creator's part to reveal his wisdom to it, and matter's part to cast off its ugliness and its lack of beauty? And this is enough for us on this subject; let us come to what remains.
'And the earth was invisible and unprepared.' When he said, 'In the beginning God made heaven and earth,' he kept silent about much: water,
air and fire, and the other affections born from them, which are what bring the world into readiness;
but Scripture left these for our minds to investigate, and by this small occasion we have been brought to consider what remains.
And since it was not said of water that God created it, while it was said of the earth that it was invisible, consider for yourself: with what covering was it covered when it did not yet appear?
It could not be covered by fire, for fire illuminates everything and does not darken.
Nor could air then be a covering for it,
for the nature of air is thin and pure, receptive of everything visible, and it allows other things to be seen.
Now then, it is evident to the mind that it was water that covered the face of the earth, and since that moist nature had not been gathered into its own place.
And it was not only for this reason that the earth was invisible, but it was also unprepared, for excessive moisture, then as now, hinders the earth from sprouting grass.
And this is the cause of its unpreparedness and its invisibility.
For the natural beauty of the earth was its being prepared;
plains waving with crops, and the green places of the gardens sending up flowers of many colors, broad valleys and mountain tops covered with trees,

of which there was then nothing of the kind upon it. And it was in labor to give birth to all this through the power of the Creator that was within it, but it was waiting for the proper times, so that it might bring forth its offspring at the command of God.
And it says: 'Darkness was upon the abysses.' Here again are occasions for vain words and [?] of godlessness, on the part of those who twist the word of Scripture according to their own minds.
For they interpret darkness not as coming from the shadow of some body, or as a place without light for some reason,
but they say that it is a power of evil, that it is itself evil, having its beginning from itself, and that it is opposed to the goodness of God.
For they said: if 'God is light,' then the power that opposes him is darkness, according to the reasoning of the mind;
and a darkness whose establishment comes from nowhere else,

but which is the begetter of itself: darkness, the warfare of souls, the worker of death and the opponent of virtue, which is found to be uncreated by God. And they led themselves astray by the word of the prophet.
And by such a saying, what evil words, estranged from God, did they not fashion?

'Like grievous wolves' among those of God, with this small word they destroyed many souls! Did not those Marcionites and Valentinians arise from here? Or did not that loathsome heresy of the Manichaeans come from here,
which someone called the corruption of the churches, and was not mistaken? Why do you flee far from the truth, O man, to the destruction of your own self?
The word, clear and understandable to all, says: 'The earth was invisible.' And what is the reason for this? Because the abyss was over the earth. And what is the abyss?
A multitude of waters, whose depth is hard to reach. And is anyone able to say: At some time we have seen many bodies, and over them there was pure and [?] water,
so why was no part of the earth visible in those waters? Because the air that lay above it was dark and invisible.
For when the brightness of the sun rests upon water, its sediment [?] becomes visible. But in the darkness of night nothing can be seen in the waters.
And what did not permit the earth to be seen was that abyss, above which there was darkness.
The abyss was not a multitude of opposing powers, nor was it a power of evil authority opposed to the good.
For when any two things are equal to one another in opposition, then they would be destroyers of one another and would forever be in endless turmoil.

And if one of them overcomes its fellow by its power, it is its destroyer. And if they say that evil is equal to good in opposition, then they introduce unceasing war and unrelenting corruption, for sometimes the one would prevail and sometimes the other.
And if the power of good always prevails, why has that power of evil not been utterly abolished?
Or if, on the contrary to this, which it is not right to say, I am amazed how they do not flee from themselves when they arrive at such godlessness and blasphemy!
And it is not at all right for a believing man to say: "The essence of evil is from God himself," for no things that are contrary to one another can establish one another.
Life does not beget death, nor is darkness the beginning of light, nor is sickness the producer of health.
But in changes of condition a contrary drives out its contrary; yet he says that those that are equal to it in kind come forth together. And again they said:
"If evil is uncreated [?], and it was not made by God either, where then does its nature come from? For no one living in this world denies evil." What then shall we say to this?
For evil is not a living and animate nature, but a movement in the soul contrary to virtue, and it arises among the negligent from a lack of good.
And do not think that evil comes from outside;
nor think that the nature of evil has existed from the first,
but each person is the beginning of his own evil.
For of the things that happen with us, some are from nature, as for example old age and weakness; and some happen suddenly from external causes,

whether distressing or gladdening, as when someone finds treasure while digging a pit, or a mad dog bites him as he goes out to trade; and some are from us, as for example restraining the soul from desire,
or letting it loose, or restraining it from anger, or strengthening the hand against one who provokes anger, or truth or falsehood, or humility or pride.
But as for that over which you have power, do not seek its causes outside, but know that true evil comes from the inclination of the will.
And if it were not from us and not from our will, punishment from the law would not be laid upon the evildoer in proportion to his deeds.
And this statement of mine concerns evil that is truly evil. But destitution [?] and infirmity and disgrace, and the other distressing circumstances of human beings,
ought not to be counted as part of evil; and the other things, the contraries of these, are not to be reckoned among us as anything greatly good,
of which some exist by nature and some befall us for the better.
But let us be silent at this time about the interpretation of darkness by way of censure [?], and let us accept its interpretation simply, following the thought of Scripture.
And let us speak about the inquiry into darkness: whether it was created together with the world, or whether it is prior to light, and why the inferior thing came first?
And we said that this darkness does not subsist by nature, but is an affection in the air, and it arises from a lack of light.
And what light was suddenly lacking to the world, so that because of this darkness came to be over the waters?
For we know that, since there was something before the creation of this perishable world, it was in light, as it indisputably was [?].
And those powers of the angels and the hosts of heaven, those that are named and those that cannot be named, of the rational natures, and the ministering spirits: all these were not in darkness,
but in light and spiritual joy and in the state of readiness that befitted them.
And no one denies this. And that is the awaited light, promised among the good things to come, about which Solomon said:

"The light of the righteous is forever." It says: "Give thanks to the Father, who has made us worthy of the portion of the inheritance of the saints in that light." If those who are condemned are sent into that outer darkness, how much more will the rest of those who do good be in that light which is greater than this world.
And when heaven was created by the command of God, it was at once spread out over all that its circumference enclosed.
And it has a vast body, and it is able to make the outer part [?] the inner part; and it involuntarily cut off the brightness of the light, and that place was left without light.
For in the establishing of a shadow these three come together: light, a body, and an unlit place.
And the darkness of the world came about from the body of heaven.
And understand this from a perceptible example. Set up for yourself a tent made firm by its thickness, right at midday, when the air is clear, and place yourself in its darkness.
Consider that darkness in the same way: it was not raised up first, but it followed upon something else.
Of this darkness it was said that it was upon the abyss, for the extremities of the air touch all visible bodies;
and water was over everything; therefore it was necessarily said: "Darkness was upon the abyss."

"And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters." If the prophet calls the expanse of this air a spirit, then accept from him the enumeration of the parts of this world, for God created heaven and earth, water and air, flowing and poured out.
And if he means the Holy Spirit of God, which is rather what is truly the case, as those before us have said,
for Scripture has specifically mentioned him, and nothing else is called the Spirit of God except the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of truth, the completer of the blessed Trinity.
And when you accept it in this way, you will find great benefit from it. And how was he moving over the waters?
I will tell you, not speaking from myself, but from what was said by a Syrian man, who was removed from the wisdom of this world and close to the knowledge of truth.

For he said that the language of the Syrians is especially clear for the interpretation of the Scriptures, because it is close to that of the Hebrews. And the interpretation, the force of this word that was spoken, is this:
"was moving" means, that is to say:
it was warming and giving life to the nature of water, as a brooding hen does, which imparts life-giving power to those she has warmed.
And he likewise said that this word signifies this meaning in what was said: "The Spirit of God was moving over the waters."
And this makes very clear what is being sought by certain people, who say that created things are brought to completion by the Holy Spirit. "And God said:

'Let there be light.' That [?] of God created the beauty of light and made light; it shattered the gloom, revealed beauty, and adorned all things. At once it brought forth a desirable sight, and that heaven,
which had been hidden by darkness, appeared.

And the eyes that behold its beauty bear witness. Now, as it appeared then, the air also rejoiced, for the light was all the more prepared within it, wholly and in everything, and it sent out the distribution of light swiftly toward all its boundaries:
upward it reached to the ether and to heaven, and in breadth it shone as far as the parts of the world in the blink of an eye, to east and west, to north and south.
For such is its nature, fine and bright, that it needs no span of time for its passage.
And just as our sight reaches its object without any lapse of time, so too it sends forth its light to its limits.

And after the light, the ether, of hot nature, is beautiful and the waters are brilliant, not only in so far as they receive the brilliance of the light, but because by that illumination of theirs they also illumine other things.

And the voice of God made every honorable preparation. Just as some people pour oil into the depth of water and that place becomes bright, so the Creator of all spoke, and at once there came to be in the world [?].
'Let there be light.' And that command became deed; that nature came to be, than which nothing is more beautiful for delight, and which human thought cannot reach.

And when we say 'the voice of the Lord,' or 'word' or 'command,' we do not mean this, that some sound comes out of a vocal organ, nor do we understand it thus, that the word of the Godhead is air that strikes upon the tongue,
but we call the inclination of his will a voice, as a matter for the understanding of learners.
'And God saw that light, that it was good.' [?] to that which was declared beforehand by the Creator to be good?

And this discourse commands our eyes to decide this, for it could not say more than the testimony of the senses. And if the essence of bodily beauty is the proportion of the limbs and the goodness of a bright color, then how does the nature of light, simple and even in its parts, not reach the limit of beauty?
For the proportion of light is not only in its parts, but in the restfulness of the gaze directed toward it.
Likewise gold does not draw the eyes to itself by the proportion of its parts, but only by the goodness of its color.
Likewise the morning star is more beautiful than the stars, not in so far as its members fit one another, but in so far as it sends out its brilliance toward our eyes without effort.

And that testimony of God concerning the good is not only on account of what pleases the gaze of the eyes, but on account of the benefit that you will attain from it in the end; for as yet there were no eyes [?] of the light.
'And God separated between that light and between the darkness,' those two being opposed to one another and unmixed,
and he separated them from each other by a distant separation.
'And God called that light day,
"And the darkness he called night": it is the air [?] the light of the sun, [?] that half of the round of heaven [?] the sun; by the shadow of the earth it becomes night.

But at that time day and night did not come about through the movement of the sun, but through the [?] of the light [?] created. "And there was evening and there was morning, the first day." Evening is the common boundary of day and night, and morning, in turn, is the neighboring of night with day. And in order to give day the first place in existence, he mentioned the end of day first, and morning is the end of night, for night follows day. But what existed before the creation of the world was not night but darkness. The opposite of day is this night, which received a new name after day. "And there was evening and there was morning."
He called that one day together with its night "day," and he did not call it "day and night," but gave the name to the one that prevails.
And this custom is found in all the books in the reckoning of times, for days are counted, and not nights along with days.
As it says in the Psalms: "The days of our years"; and again Jacob says:
"The days of our life are few and wretched." In the words of the books, the phrase "the days of our life" is used in this same way.
"And there was evening, and there was morning, one day." Why did he not say,
"It was the first day"? Instead he said:
"It was one day"?
And it is like someone who would say [?]
Discourse of the same, chapter three, of the third discourse [?], as it is said in the Psalms,
for "Your words are sweet to my palate, more than honey to my mouth." It was possible [?] your souls with the word of God,
and we have come on this second day to see the wonders of [?], which were made on that second day.
And it is not unknown to me how many manual laborers, who earn their food day by day,
are present here and are looking for the sermon to be shortened, so that they may not be kept away from their work. And I say to them
that every [?] that is lent to God is not lost to the one who lends it, but is repaid to him many times over.

And every circumstance that causes preoccupation the Lord will drive away, and he will grant strength to the body, diligence to the soul, and success in trade throughout all of life to those who choose what is spiritual. Even if they have no hope in this world,
yet that teaching of the Holy Spirit is their treasure for what is to come.
And now cast out of your heart every care of this world and gather your mind toward me.
For the body is of no benefit when the mind is not free, being caught up in the agitation of the world.
"And God said: Let there be a firmament dividing between waters and waters." [?] of God: "Let there be light," and today we have heard: "Let there be a firmament."
And at this point it appears that he has added something to the word, for that word did not stop at a small matter,
But it indicated the purpose of the firmament and said: that it may divide between waters and waters.

But first let us inquire how the Lord speaks: is it perhaps in our manner? For an impression of something forms in our minds, and then, after reflection, we choose what signifies [?]; and we convey it from the mind by the vocal instruments, by striking the air,

and we make manifest, by the movement of the gathered voice, [?] what is hidden in our commands. But whoever says of God that he needs such a procedure to make known what is to be understood is a liar.
It is far more credible to say that the will of God and the first impulse of the movement of his mind is the word of God.

But Scripture spoke in this way to indicate that he wished not only the existence of created things, but also to create them with a helper. And it could have spoken as it did about the beginning of everything:
"In the beginning God made heaven and earth," so that it might have said:
"God created light" and "God created the firmament." But when it says that God commanded and said, by this it indicated, with a hidden earnestness, the one who was commanded and addressed by him.
It is not that it begrudges us knowledge, but it makes us long for the will of God, through which it shows us a trace and an inexpressible image,
for what is gained through labor is received with joy and guarded with diligence, while that which is easily found is despised.
For this reason it raises us by a path and in due order to the knowledge of the only-begotten Son.
And that bodiless nature has no need of a vocal word, for what is first conceived in thought is powerfully present with the helper.
What need, then, is there of words for those who are partners in counsel?
For voice was made for the sense of hearing, and hearing for voice. And where there is neither air nor tongue,
nor ear, nor the winding canal leading to the head, the organ for perceiving sounds, there no word is needed, but rather the path of the will from the thoughts of the heart.
And in order to rouse our mind to inquire to whom the word is addressed, it adopted this image of speech with careful preparation and wisdom.
And secondly, let us ask whether this firmament, which was called heaven, is the heaven that was created first, or not. Or are there two heavens, or not?
For those who philosophized about heaven would more easily cut out their tongues than truly accept this. For they say: "Heaven is one, and its nature does not allow that there should be a second,
or a third, or many, for all of its matter has been used up in its being.

And how could there be, in a spherical body, which has its limit from that [?], a second or a third from it?" This is the argument of those who introduce alongside God an uncreated density, poured out by their vanity into falsehood.
And we beseech the wise men of the pagans not to reproach us before putting their own affairs in order.
For there are some among them who speak of many heavens and many worlds. When these are refuted for their evil argument with powerful reasoning and by the compelling force of measurement,
that the heaven has no nature but one only, then let us mock their wayward verbosity, since they see
that for this reason there are [?] those bubbles swelling up on the waters, many and one, and they have doubted, saying that the power of God is unable to establish many heavens,
whose power and extent are no greater before God than that bubble which forms on the water beneath a stream of water.

And so that statement of theirs, when they say, "It is impossible," is laughable. But we, although we accept two heavens, seek a third as well, the one that holy Paul, who was made worthy to see it, mentioned. And this is no more astonishing than those seven circles
in which those seven stars travel, according to the agreement of all accounts, and which are fitted to one another in the manner of a tube,
bound to one another;
And they move in a course contrary to the whole. The ether is parted before them, and they give out a beautiful sound to the ears [?] [?] [?] of pleasures [?].

And when [?] [?] [?] [?], something indicative of the [?] word among the senses, what did they say? They said that because of our first habit we have been forced to become used to hearing the sound. Since we have been accustomed to it from birth, this perception has gone from us, like those
whose ears have been dulled by the noise of the blacksmiths.

And the refutation of those feeble devices of theirs is evident to everyone from their very first word, and they do not need a man who knows how to be sparing of time and is careful of the understanding of his hearers.
But let us leave the outsiders to the outsiders and come to the teaching of the Church. Some before us have said
that [?] [?] [does not ?] [?] the creation of a second heaven, but is an explanation of the first. For there it was said briefly that in the beginning God made heaven and earth,
and here he has explained the statement, in order to tell us how each of them was created.
But we say that, since it has another name, its very function is also something else, and it is not that heaven created first, and that it has a firm nature.
It provides what is useful to all things. "And God said: Let there be a firmament among the waters, and let it be a divider between waters and waters.
And God made the firmament. And he separated between the waters that were beneath the firmament and the waters
that are above the firmament." And before we approach the meaning of the scripture, let us hasten to refute the argument that [?] bring. Some have asked us:
if the shape of the firmament is round, as our sight indicates, and water by nature flows and slips down from a height,
"How could it stay on the back of the firmament?" And we say: not everything that looks round from below must necessarily follow

to be round on top as well, like something that is fully vaulted. We see that the vaults of bathhouses and of caves hollowed out [?] [?] are round on the inside, but their upper side is sometimes flat.
And therefore let them not wear out us or themselves, as if we were unable to keep waters on the upper side.

And after this let us say what the nature of the firmament is, and for what reason it was commanded that it be among the waters. It is the custom of Scripture to call [?] great in strength "firmament," as the psalm says:
"I have established its pillars" by his power: that solid, firm, full body, according to the measure of that account [?],
whose being consists only in extension, in length and breadth and depth, without solidity, and [?] kind [?],
whose being consists in extension and solidity.

And it is the custom of Scripture to call everything hard and unceasing a "firmament," as is said at times of the air when it thickens: "who makes firm the thunders." Because of the wind that remains in the clouds, when it is released with difficulty, with that sound that makes the thunder, Scripture spoke of the firmness of thunder.
And we know that the nature of water, soft and flowing, has been made firm into a hard and solid nature by the power of that commanding voice.
And it is not right for us to think, as many do, that the firmness of the firmament comes from water, or in any way resembles frozen water. Therefore let us suppose
that the beginning of its being is from the thickening of moisture, like the crystal stone,
which comes from the excessive freezing of the water of the earth; and it changes, as they say, into a nature that they call sphekla [?], which is found in certain places.
And that stone is brilliant, and it has great purity and clarity.
And when it is found pure in its own nature, with no corrosion or hollowness in it, it resembles the air in its purity.
And now let us not liken the firmament to anything of this kind. For this is a childish and feeble thought, if we suppose any such thing about heaven.
Nor even insofar as everything is in everything, that is, fire in earth and air in waters, and many other things one within another.
And there is nothing among material things subject to the senses that is unmixed with another.

Therefore we say that the essence of the firmament is of one of the simple substances, or of those simple substances combined. And Scripture has taught us not to apply our minds to examining everything, as far as they reach.
And let us not neglect this: that after God's command that there be a firmament, Scripture did not say:
"And the firmament came to be," but it said: "The Lord made the firmament," and, completely: "He separated it."
O you deaf, hear, and you blind, see! And who is deaf, except the one who has not heard the words of the Holy Spirit?
And who is blind, except the one who could not see the clear teachings about the only-begotten Son of God?

"Let there be a firmament": this is the voice of the first, originating cause! "And God made the firmament": this is a testimony to the creating and fashioning power! But let us turn our discourse back to the remaining exposition.
"And let it be a separator between waters and waters."

So far does the flow of water extend, covering the earth on every side and surging over it, that it may even be supposed to be greater than all material things. For this reason it was said at first: "The abyss was upon the earth."
And next let us speak again about the reason for the abundance of the waters.
And I do not think that anyone among the careful, those who look minutely into this flowing and perishable nature, would reproach you, saying: "We have taken up an argument that is impossible";
nor let us be challenged as to what the nature of the waters was made firm upon.
For just as the earth is heavier than water, and it is said that it suspends it in the middle and that it is set apart from the edges,
so too they acknowledge that that great mass of water is immovable, because of its downward motion and its even inclination toward the earth from every side.
So then the nature of water was poured out abundantly upon the earth, not merely to its measure, but many times more than it,
for the great Maker arranged it for its final use.
And what need is there for this untold abundance of waters? For it is of necessity needed with respect to the nature of fire, not only for the ordering of the earth,
but for the completion of everything. And if all of it were lacking in something that is most needful of all, it would indeed be deficient.
For these are opposed to and destructive of one another: fire of water, when it prevails in power, and water of fire, when it exceeds in abundance.
And it was indeed fitting that the lack of one should not become the cause of the destruction of everything.
And for the ordering of all this, he stored up the abundance of waters of the ordering, so that it might suffice for the stability of the world in holding back the nature of that fire,

to be consumed by it little by little until the time that God has appointed for the world. For God, by whom the drops of rain are numbered, knows how many times have been appointed for the world, or how much of the water needs to be stored up for that fire as what it needs.
And this is the account of the existence of the abundance of waters!
And no one among people who are in this life denies that the world of necessity needs fire. It is not only for the works that serve our life that fire is needful,
such as weaving and carpentry and smithing and farming,
but trees too would neither put forth branches nor ripen fruit, nor [?] of the land and of the water, nor could they grow or endure for any length of time, if heat were not present.
So then this need for heat is indeed a necessity for the firm standing of existing things; the abundance of moisture is of necessity needed for fire, for it can by no means be held off.
And you may see the heat of fire prevailing over everything that is born and decays.
For this reason the waters are poured out abundantly upon the earth and even farther than this visible expanse. And again it is sown beneath all the depths of the earth.
For this reason there are unfailing springs and gushing wells and rivers of water, so that it may be a treasury of moisture.

For this reason the water of India, greater than all waters, flows from the east, as some of those who travel far have told us. And again in the mid-east there is a river called the Bactrus; and another river called the Skholebis, and another,
which [?] Araxes, and from this river there comes out [?] another river, which is called the Tanais, and it goes down into the lake that is called Maeotis.
And along with this is the river called the Phasis, which pours down from the summits of the Caucasus mountains; and many others on the northern side pour into that deep which is called the Euxine.
And on the western side, beneath the mountain called the Pyrenees, come forth the rivers called the Tartessus and the Ister;
and one of them goes down into the sea that is outside the boundaries of Hercules, while the Ister passes along through Europe and pours into the sea of Pontus.
And how many of the rivers should I count that come from the mountains of Scythia? Among them are the river called Orodanos and Orentis, together with many other rivers,
on which ships travel toward the inland Galatians and toward the Celts and toward the barbarians who are near the mountain, and it goes down into the western sea.

But as for those on the southern side, in upper Ethiopia, some of them pour down into this sea of ours, and some outside this navigable sea: the rivers called Agon and Nosis, and the river named Bremetis,
and with them the Nile, which by its nature is not like a river when it spreads out over Egypt.
Thus the place where people dwell is clothed with very great seas and many rivers by the inexpressible wisdom of the one who governs the nature that opposes fire, so that it may not be lacking.
And at some time everything will be dried up by fire, as Isaiah said in that counsel of God: 'I am
the one who says to the deep, Be laid waste, and to all your rivers, Dry up.' And accept that thought of true teaching, for although it is unlearned in speech, yet it is not weak in thought.
'Let there be a firmament among the waters, and let it be a separator between water and water.'

Now it has been said what the book indicated concerning the name of the firmament; for it did not call a dry, solid and heavy nature a firmament, and if that were so, the earth would surely be more worthy of this naming,
But because the nature above is fine and thin and cannot be reached by the senses, he called it "firmament" by comparing it with the fine things that fall under the senses.

And consider the place that separates and distributes moisture. Whatever part of it is fine and purified, it sends upward. Whatever part is thick and earthy, it sends out toward all things. In this way the balance stays in place from first to last, as the moisture lessens little by little.
But you deny the abundance of the waters and do not consider the abundance of fire, which, although small in size, yet consumes many waters.
It drinks up the moisture that is in front of it, like a cupping-glass [?]. It also consumes what it has drawn up, just as the flame of a lamp does,
which draws up its nourishment and consumes it at once.
And as for the air, who could disbelieve that it is hot and burning?

And if it were not held fast, against its will, by the determination of its Creator, what would prevent it from burning up everything [?] above it? A cloud forms [?] in that place through the rising of the vapor of rivers and lakes, so that the ether may not overheat and burn.
And let us look at a wet place at the time when such places dry up: what has become of that water? Was it not that heat which dissipated it?
And with all this they do not admit that the sun is hot, those idle talkers, whatever reasoning they rely on; and they make an argument and say that:
Its color is white, and not red or ruddy; therefore it is not hot by nature.
And again they also say this: The heat comes from its great motion.
And by this they mean that the sun does not destroy moisture. But as for me, even if that statement is true, [?] of the waters is, even involuntarily, needed [?] on account of that heat.
And it makes no difference in this matter whether the heat is by nature or from some affection, if pieces of wood by rubbing against one another produce fire, and a flame burns by its blazing,
but the end of both of these lies with the Governor of all; he moves the sun from place to place,
so that it may not stay in one place and, by the intensity of its heat, destroy that one region.
For this reason, in the winter season and at other times, it moves to the places where days and nights are equal,
and from there, in the summer season, it moves to the northern regions. In this way the region of the earth is balanced by its proper tempering, through the movement of the sun.
And they do not retract their own statement, but say that nothing is added to the sea from the rivers, for when the sun drinks up from the sea the sweet, drinkable part,
the sea remains salty in character, thin and bitter and briny; and then they turn around and say that:
The sun [?] nothing of the water.
`And God called the firmament by the name heaven.' Truly the name befits another, and this one resembles it by name.
And we have seen that Scripture in many places gives this name to the visible and high place, as when it says:
`The birds of heaven' and `that which flies in the firmament of heaven' and `they [?] to the heavens and go down to the abysses.' Moses, when he blessed the tribe of Joseph, said:
"From the boundaries of heaven and from its dew,
and from the declining of the sun and the gathering of the moons, and from the peaks of the mountains and from the fruitful hills may a blessing be given to you." When it is tempered,
it is fruitful. In your curses [?] their bronze altogether [?], from which the earth bears fruits.
And when it says that dew or rain comes down from heaven, let us understand that those waters are established above.
For vapors [?], and the air becomes dense through the pressing of the winds, and it scatters the moisture within the clouds,
[?] its heaviness it turns into drops, and it rushes down toward the earth; and this is the substance of rain.
And when the moisture is [?] by the violence of the winds, and then they shrivel [?] and freeze from that great cold, and then the cloud is scattered, then snow falls.
And of this same [?] in all the creation of moisture, which are above, over our heads.
And let no one compare the simplicity of the spiritual saying with the saying of the babblers, who philosophize about the heaven.
For just as the beauty of virginity is greater than the beauty of harlotry, so great is the difference between our saying and the saying of those outsiders.
For the persuasiveness of their saying comes by constraint, but here the truth is set forth without contrivance.

And what need do we have to weary ourselves in refuting their falsehood? It is enough that you take their books and compare them with one another calmly, for you will see their opposition to one another.
And they are no fewer in number than one another, in the mutual opposition of their thinking [?]; they say
that everything is burned up and comes to life again from what was left remaining in the burnt remains. They speak endlessly [?] away from the truth; on every side they find [?] toward their error.
And we also have a word addressed to the churches concerning the separation of the waters,

to those who, out of loftiness of speech [?], say that in parable these are spiritual and incorporeal powers, and that the good among them have remained above the firmament, while the evil have gone to the places of the earth and of density.
For this reason it is said in the psalm: 'Waters above the heavens, praise the form [?] of the Lord'; because of the purity of their mind they were made worthy to give glory to God.

But those waters, they say, which are the wicked spirits, have fallen away from the honor of their nature to the pit [?] of evil; and they are [?] because of their turmoil, and because of the turmoil of passion they were called a raging sea, on account of their changeableness and the turmoil of their stirring, on account of their reproach [?].
And let us cast this saying away like a dream and old-womanish [?]; they are waters, and let us accept the division that is beneath the firmament according to the reason stated.
Although it is said that they praise the Lord of all, do not think that they have a soul, even though 'they declare the glory of God.' Nor is the firmament a living, knowing creature,
even though they declare 'the creation, the work of his hands.' If someone should say that when it says 'heavens' [?], and by 'firmament' it means the active powers [?], as is fitting;

we too shall accept this saying as well prepared, but we shall in no way reckon the nature of dew and mist and frost and heat as intelligent and invisible, for Daniel commanded them, but by way of saying [?] that they are accomplishers of the glory of the Creator.
and it is not that the water above the heavens was honoured for its virtue and raised up,
and glorifies God because of its height. Rather, the book [?] says 'the deeps that are of the earth' [?]. That deep,
which people who speak this way have cast down to the worst place, the psalm did not exclude from glorifying God. That deep too, in its own way [?], carries out the glorification of the Creator.
'And God saw
that it was good.' Not that the works of God delight his eyes, nor is his approval of the good
As [?] our acceptance [?]; rather, it is good in his sight because it is well made and well fitted together,
which is why it is said that the one who intended to create all things was pleased beforehand with the work of the parts, since by the measure of his wisdom they bring the whole to completion.
Likewise, when its [?] limbs have been scattered, and someone then sees them set in their proper order, its beauty will become clear even to the unskilled [?].
But its maker, even before its limbs are gathered together, knows the beauty of each of them individually, for the heart [?] of God, as if to say: now he has praised the works of the parts,
and again he will receive fitting praise for the world. And let our discourse on the second day be enough. Let the diligent listeners have time to examine what they have heard;

and whatever profit there may be in it, let them preserve it by remembrance and diligent reflection, and let them await the profit. In the affairs of the world let them be at leisure [?], and may evening find them purified of their thoughts [?].
And may God, who created such great things, and who arranged that these few words be spoken, give you understanding of the truth,
so that you may see the invisible from the visible, and by the vastness and beauty of created things may glorify the Creator. His [?] is plainly visible in his creatures,
as are the beginninglessness of his power and his divinity, he who is our benefactor through earth and air, and heaven and water, and day and night.
And let us give no time to sin, but [?] [be filled] with the things of God among us always, and with the remembrance of him,
to whom belongs all glory and might forever and ever. [?] (abbreviation 'st~kni', possibly 'Amen')

Spoken by the same [author]. Chapter [?]. Some cities feed [their people] with marvellous spectacles in the light [?] from morning until evening. The sweetness of voices also produces much corruption in their souls, yet the listeners can never get enough of it. Many people call that assembly blessed, the hours of their life [spent] in handwork [?],
which were set apart for them in pleasures and dissipation, as if [?]. Corrupt spectacles, and the fruit [?] and display of dancing, are a school of corruption for many.

those who become attached to it. And the sounds of pipes are a delight of fornication, when they settle in the souls of those who hear them. And many are lovers of the racecourse; their folly does not leave them [?].
But we, whom the Wonderworker has called to see his works, for seeing, or for hearing the words of the Holy Spirit [?].

Let us instead reflect on the work of the great God. Let us call to mind the times that are past and look at the beauty of all things: how the heaven stands like a vault, as the prophet says, and the earth,
beyond telling in breadth and weight, [rests] upon itself; soft and moist [?] it breathes [?] it,
which parts before one who walks through it and does not hinder those who enter upon them.
And again let us look at the nature of water, some of it sweet and some of another kind, which has been prepared for our other needs,
and at its tranquil gathering in appointed places, as we have just read: 'And God said:
Let these waters that are under heaven gather into their gathering-place, and let the dry land appear. And it was so; and the water gathered, and the dry land appeared.
And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the waters he called seas.' Within [?] the cause,
From what was it invisible [?] falls upon, when sight falls upon every perceptible color!?
And perhaps it will not be enough for you to say that it was invisible not by nature, but only invisible to us, because water covered the face of all the earth.
Now hear the Scripture [?], how it reveals itself: Let the waters be gathered and let the dry land appear.
Let the curtains be drawn back, so that what was invisible may appear. And perhaps someone may inquire about this, asking why it was said
that by God's command water came to flow upward, since such is itself the nature of water?

For as long as water is on some level ground and has no channel, it stands still; in a sloping place it swiftly rushes down, and by it [?] draws along what follows it, in the measure of its weight and in the measure of the slope of the place to which it flows.
And since water is by nature like this, the words 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering' are surely superfluous.
For since its nature is to go downward, even without willing it, it would flow down to the deepest place, and it would not stop flowing until it was leveled.
And are there not some [?] who also say again: How was it commanded the waters to be gathered into one gathering, when, behold, we see many seas, each distinct and separate?
And let us speak about that first statement: that you cannot know, O reader, the movement of the waters except as restless after God's command, and by nature it goes down to cavernous places;
and how it was able to reach such a height before God's command, you have neither seen nor heard from anyone who might have seen it.
And understand that this voice of God is the creator of natures, and the command that was given among created things at that time is the same one that stands established among created things forever.
It was said once that day and night should be created, and from then until now they alternate and divide [?]. Let the waters be gathered:
the nature of the waters was commanded to run and never [?] from it.
I say this because I see the movement of the waters. For some flow immediately of their own accord, like springs and rivers, and some stand gathered.
But what I am saying here concerns the rivers.

Let the waters be gathered into one gathering. When you see a spring that sends up a great quantity of water, consider in your mind who it is that sends up that water from the womb of the earth, or who it is that [?] toward it in the forward direction?
Or from what treasuries does it come forth? And to where does it hasten, or how are they not filled? These things depend on that first voice, and from there too comes their end.
So then, whenever you see water, remember that first voice that spoke thus: Let the waters be gathered.
And it was fitting that they should be gathered into their place, and when they reach their appointed places [?], and for this reason 'all created things [?] and into the sea,

and the sea is not sated,' as Ecclesiastes says. For the flowing of the waters is by God's command, and the confining of the sea by its boundary comes from the first voice. Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.
So that the flowing water might not overflow, shift from its own place, fill everything and submerge it: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering."
For this reason the sea is stirred up by the wind and rises in waves. And as it comes near the sand of the shore, God said through the prophet:
"Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who [?] of the sea" — there is nothing at all [?] that would prevent the Red Sea from coming over Egypt.

For Egypt lies lower than the depths of the sea that are near [?] it. Was the sea not fettered by the command of its Creator? And [?] of the land of Egypt, by those who wanted to join together the sea of Egypt and the sea of India, which is the Red Sea, and they could not do it.

First Sesostris [?] Darius intended [?]. The power of God: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering," that is: let them not pass from here to anywhere else, but let them remain in the gathering. And "let the waters be gathered into one gathering" indicated that the waters were abundant and scattered in many ways. For the ravines of the mountains were full of water, and the sloping valleys were not lacking in depth.
And many other forms of the land and depths were full of water, and into one gathering [?].
And let no one say: if there was water above, the places which afterward received the seas [?].
And since these were full, as we might say, of waters, when he commanded that they be gathered together [?].
For not [?], nor that terrifying deep which sailors do not dare to approach, which surrounds the island of Britain and the western Iberians,
but they were created at that time and spread out by the command of God.
And if anyone should say, "We see from experience the opposite of Scripture, for the waters are not gathered in one place, but [?] and plainly": the opposing [?] and the places,
in which rainwater collects,

cannot refute this statement of ours. Rather, he called that great and complete gathering the "one gathering." Pits too are gatherings of waters, formed when moisture from the ground collects in the dug-out hollow. So now not every [?] of Scripture, but that great and greatest gathering,

in which the whole element is seen. [?] it is divided into portions and poured out here and there [?], and likewise the air is divided finely, and all of it at once is poured out over the region of the earth.
So too water: although it is divided into small gatherings, yet the great gathering, which is the element, is what the word of Scripture indicates.
And lakes in one region and in the region of Pontus are called gatherings, but here it speaks of that gathering which is greater than all, and which is equal to the earth in its size.
But although these are full of water, and that water is salty like that of the great sea, it is not called an element, as with the Dead Sea,
which is in Judea, and the lake called Serbon, which is between Egypt [?], as certain far travellers have related to us, that these certain [?],

That the Hyrcanian sea [?] are surrounded [?]; but as the geographers have written, they are connected to one another and also to the great sea, just as they say of the Red Sea that it communicates with the sea that lies beyond Gadeira [Cádiz]. And if anyone asks why Scripture says that he called the gathering of the waters "seas", let him know, then,
that the waters gathered into one gathering, but its gulfs, which remained in their own shapes upon the earth, God called seas, as for example,
the sea of the north and the sea of the south, and the sea of the east and the sea of the west, and the particular names of the deeps:
the deep of the Euxine and of the Propontis and of the Hellespont and of the Aegean and of the Ionian,
and the deep of Sardinia, the Tyrrhenian — the enumeration now grows too long for us. For this reason God called that gathering [?]. [?] has brought us here; let us stay here [?].
And God said: Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.
And he did not say, 'Let the earth appear,' so as not to show it unprepared, while it was still mud and mixed with water and had not yet received its adornment and power;
and again, so that we should not suppose that its dryness came from the sun, for this reason the Creator made its dryness before the sun.
Understand in your mind what is written: for not only the great mass of waters upon the earth, but also that which was within its density came out, in obedience to that unfailing command.
And it was so. This following phrase is enough to teach that the voice of God became deed.
And in certain books it is written that:
The waters which were under heaven were gathered into their gathering, and the dry land appeared. And none of the translators has given us this, nor is it superfluous [?], for it testifies many times
that it came to pass thus; but in the corrected copies a mark is drawn over this statement,
and the lifting up signifies destruction [?]. And God called the dry land earth.
For dryness is a property and the character of the underlying nature, whereas 'earth' is only a slight name for a thing, in the same way as:
rationality is proper to a human being, whereas 'human' is a word indicating the living creature in which rationality exists.
Likewise dryness is the property of earth, and that which has dryness as its own was called earth, just as that which neighs was called a horse.
And this is so not only with earth, but other things too have a quality by which each is known from another.
And the quality of water is properly coldness, and of air [?], of fire — heat.
But these [?] are, and those which have become bodies and have received the quality [?], then, the perceptible [?] of those mentioned, released [?] and not alone, but earth is dry and cold,
and air is hot and moist, and fire is hot and dry.

And thus, through conjoined qualities, there arises the power of mixture of everything, each with all, and through blending with its opposite it is [?] also cold, and it mixes with water through the nearness of coldness,
and earth through water mixes with air,
For water is between the two of them, and holds their condition as if by the hand: coldness from water, and moisture; air, through the mediation of natures [?] of fire,

and it mingles with water through moisture and with fire through heat. [Fire] is by nature hot and dry, and it joins with air through heat, and again returns to communion, and thus a circle comes about, fitted together by the blending of everything in everything.

And for this reason they were called fitted-together matter. And I have said this in order to indicate the reason why God called the dry land earth, and not the earth dry land. For dryness is not something [added] upon the earth, but from the very beginning it was what filled out the matter of the earth. And that which is the cause of the establishment of a being is prior by nature and more honorable than things newly appeared. The distinguishing property of the earth is prior.
'And God saw that it was good.'
This saying does not indicate that the sea was something for God to look at,
for the Creator does not behold the beauty of the earth with eyes. The sea is a thing to look at
when it is at rest, and when, from the breeze of calm, it does not strike its neighbor [literally: brother], but embraces it in peace;
but the Scripture is not to be understood in this way as saying 'good'; rather, that goodness is judged with respect to its creation.
First, because everything that sprouts from the earth comes from the sea, when it comes forth, as the shallow, cavernous places show us; for the sea,

when it is stirred by the wind and pours out through many winding outlets, and cleaves the face of the earth and comes outside, is strained and sweetened of its saltiness and bitterness. And sometimes that sea water comes out at an outlet

according to the condition [of the place], from the heat of the places [?], and comes out hot in many islands and places along the seashore. And near it there is sweet water. But by this small matter let us learn about very great things.
For so it happens with them. And let me say that water also travels within it from the shores of the sea, through hidden channels.
And the sea is good before its God, [?] under its thickness [?], that vessel of the rivers, and it receives torrents from every side, and it remains within its own boundary. And again it is good,
for it is the beginning and source of the waters of the air,
for when they are warmed by the blazing of the sun, its fine part rises with the vapor, and when it reaches the upper region and is cooled by the shade, it comes down upon the earth as rain.

And if anyone does not accept this, let him look at the [?] that are over the fire, for sometimes, when the moisture rises [?]; and again, sailors at sea, when water runs short, boil sea water and catch its vapor with a sponge, and comfort themselves with it in their distress.
[?] Again the sea is good to God, for it surrounds the islands, and it is their beauty and security.
And again, through it land becomes near to land by the unceasing voyaging of sailors, and the gaining of wealth for merchants, and there are many other causes for the benefit of this life,
and for exporting from cities whatever is surplus in them, and again for receiving what they need from another place.
And how could I be one who seeks to see the sea as it is seen before the eyes of its Creator?

And if the sea is good and praiseworthy before God, how is this assembly of the church not better, in which the prayer of fathers and of children is mingled together, like a surging wave, toward our Lord? And by a righteous stillness, [?] those who could not shake your faith with their words.
May you be worthy of being accepted by God, and keepers of this order and beauty always, through Christ Jesus our Lord, whose is the glory for ever and ever, amen. Lines: 443.
Discourse of the same, chapter five. "And God said: Let the earth bring forth the green of grass, seed for sowing according to its kind, and fruit-bearing trees according to their kind,
whose fruit shall be in itself." [?] of the weight of the water, the command came to it,
that it should first bring forth green plants, and after that we see it come to be.
For the voice and the command that was given then became, as it were, a law of nature,

and it was established upon the earth, and it gives the earth the power to give birth and bear fruit in the times to come. "Let the earth bring forth green herbage." For the beginning of a plant's growth is sprouting, and when it has sprouted a little,
it is called [?]; it develops little by little until it reaches the bringing forth of seed. "Let the earth bring forth the green of grass," that is:

Let the earth bring forth green plants of itself, and let it have no need of help from anyone anywhere. For some supposed that the sun is the cause of the existence of plants, that by drawing with its heat it makes them sprout.
And for this reason the beauty of the earth was created before the sun, so that those who have gone astray might cease from serving the sun on account of the saying that:
it is the cause of their life. When they believe

that everything had already been prepared before the sun came into existence, let them cease from their wonder at it, for in its existence it is younger than the green grass. Now then, was provision made for the beasts, and were we not worthy of care? No, but truly,
he who prepared for oxen and horses what is theirs has all the more stored up wealth and delight for you. He who feeds your livestock, the same will make grow what is needful [?] and of grass,
so that it may be food for human beings.
"Let the earth bring forth the green of grass, seed for sowing according to its kind." So that even though some grass is set apart for other creatures,

yet its benefit also comes to us, and the yield of seeds is appointed for us. And so this saying is to be understood, and Scripture says: "Let the earth bring forth the green of grass, seed for sowing after its own kind."
And in this way the wording fits, and in this way the ordering of nature is recognized: [?] is, and then the green plant,
and then the growing up; its completion is the seed.
As the saying says that everything which the earth brings forth is seed-bearing: the stalk,
and mint and saffron,
and garlic and rush and many other kinds of grass are so; for this reason the power of its seed is in the root, in the manner of the reed:
For each year, when it grows, it produces some small thing at its root, and that is the power of its seed for the second year, [?] those whose power of seed is in their roots.
And truly everything has a seed, or else a seminal power within it, "each according to its kind," it says.
For the offshoot of the reed does not produce olives; [?] it comes forth, and from seeds it springs up according to the likeness of the seed.
And everything that the earth sprouted at the first creation has been preserved until now through the continuance of the kinds. "Let the earth bring forth," it says.

Consider how, from a small voice and a brief command, the dry earth [?] its own garment of mourning, and in place of mourning put on a shining garment, and sang out for joy by bringing forth many plants.
I wish to establish among you a sense of wonder at created things, so that wherever you are, and whichever of the green plants you see, the remembrance of the Creator may be clear within you.
When you see the green grass and its flower, think about human nature, that:

"All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass" — a true image of a human lifetime. So too a man, with flesh and a body thickened by luxury, and with the shining colour of his youth,
and vigorous and strong in his movements,

after this withers with the passing of time; or else, though many petitioners and friends who make a show of friendship surround him and serve him for his good fortune, and many relatives and still more followers, some of them for bread and some for other needs, and he goes about envied in the city of his kinsmen [?],
or for command over troops, and the herald cries out on his behalf, and sword-bearers stand by, and he drives people on with torments,

and the hearts of men are full of fear of him; yet a single fever, or a pain in the side, or of the lung, snatches him away from among men and he departs, and at once all that delight of his vanishes,
and that glory of his passes away like a dream.
And truly the prophet spoke that parable, in which he likened everything of man to flowers.
"Let the earth bring forth what is sown, kind by kind and likeness by likeness." To this day the order of plants bears witness to that first creation. For sprouting comes before all grass.
if it comes up from a root, like the crocus and the reed,
it first comes out and then shoots upward; and if it comes from seed, that too first sprouts, and after this it becomes green seed [?], when it [?]. "Let the earth bring forth green grass."

When the seed falls into the earth, in which there is warmth and moisture together and in equal measure, that seed rots and becomes thin and loosened, and it seizes for itself what is proper to it from the earth.
And when the fine matter of the earth enters into that single [seed] [?] part, it then shoots up above, and the number of the upper part of its stalk corresponds to that of the roots below.
And what has come up grows warm and draws moisture from the roots;
and by the drawing power of the heat it takes from the earth whatever nourishment there is for the wheat, for the husk of the wheat, and for the awn.
And it increases little by little,

until what belongs to the seeds is brought to completion. And one green shoot or one blade of grass is enough to occupy your mind in contemplating the Creator: how the stalk of wheat has girded on its nodes as belts, so that it may bear the weight.
of the head [of grain], when it is full of wheat and bends down toward the earth.

For this reason nature has protected it with the husk [?] as with a binding, so that birds may not carry it off, and with the sharpness of the awns it wards off harm from small creatures. What shall I say, or why [?] so many, so many [?]? "Let the earth bring forth green grass."
And together with those foods there came forth also what is deadly: with the wheat hemlock, which is evil, and with the other foods lemi [?] and mandrake and things like them.
And why do we not acknowledge the gift of good and useful things, but blame him for those things that are destructive of our life?
Rather let us consider that not everything was created for the sake of our belly.
For those among them that are foods are known to all, and every created thing has its own property in its nature.

Is it not so that, however much [?] it is a killer to you, God should not for this reason have refrained from creating that animal, or should have created it as a bloodless animal, whose strength is needed for this life of ours? And the mind
that dwells in you is sufficient for you for guarding against those deadly things. It is fitting,
if sheep know what is harmful to them and guard against it by this sense, that reason and the art of healing,
which shows you what is useful, and what you have tested beforehand as harmful to itself [?],
None of these was created as evil and useless.
Some of them serve as food for us through physicians, for illnesses.
Starlings feed on hemlock, for the nature of their bodies escapes the deadly effect, since the passages of their hearts are narrow,
and their nature [?] it before its coldness has yet reached their hearts. And that plant: the particular character of their constitution escapes its harm.
And these are sometimes useful to us as well: sometimes they bring on sleep with mandrake, and they soothe the severe pains of the body with opium.

And many have cured insatiable appetite for food with hemlock, and have driven out long-standing diseases with ambrosia [?]. Those things that served for accusing their Creator are a cause of great thanksgiving among his favors. "Let the earth bring forth green plants of grass."
How many kinds of grass and fruits are there that spring up of themselves! And some had a sowing and became green,
and then reached completion in seed, so that [?] the first command may be a teaching of nature for the movement to come.
And if anyone should say: How does the earth bring forth seed according to seed, when we have reaped black grain?

let him know that it has been changed [?] into a seed, but it is rather an illness and rottenness of the seed. For it could not cast off from itself the nature of wheat, but it turned black from frost, as its name indicates.
And so far did it turn to another color and another taste.
And it is said that if it is sown again in good ground, and temperate air comes down upon it, it returns again to that former nature.

And you will find nothing that could stand against the command of God. As for tares and other foreign seeds that are mixed in with the seeds for food, they do not come from a transformation of wheat, and they have their own kind.
And they resemble those who pervert the teaching of Christ and do not become disciples of the word in purity,
But they have corrupted, by their evil teaching, the living body of the Church, so that they may secretly sprinkle their own disease upon innocent hearts.
And the Lord brought in the growth of seeds as a parable for those who believe in him, and said: "When a man sows seed in the earth and lies down,
and rises, day and night, and the seed grows, and he does not know how,
for the earth of itself brings forth the seed: first the blade, then the head, and then the full wheat in the head." "Let the earth bring forth green grass."
And in the twinkling of an eye the earth began to bring forth, so that the laws of the Creator might be kept, and it became productive of every kind.
And they became [?] of green plants, and the fruitful fields waved like the deeps with the motion of the swaying heads.
And every grass and every seed of herbs [grew] fruitfully; there was no deficiency, neither through the idleness of farmers, nor through the bad temper of the weather,
nor through any other destructive cause. Nor yet did punishment hinder the earth from bringing forth fruit,
for this was before the sin for which we were condemned to eat bread by the sweat of our face.
"And the fruitful and fruit-bearing tree, whose seed is in it, seed-bearing always."
By this word all the thickets multiplied and all the trees rose high in stature: fir and cypress; and all the plants became [?] laurels according to their kinds,
and each of them has the adornment by which it is recognized.
But the rose was without thorns, and only afterward was the thorn joined to the calyx of the flower,
so that sorrow might be close to the pleasure of desire, and so that we might remember the sin for which the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles. And if anyone should say
that the earth was commanded to bring forth a fruitful tree, [?] whose seed is in it,
and yet behold, we do not see fruit on all trees, and not for this reason, that:

those that are honorable by nature were worthy of being mentioned first; and again, if you examine carefully, you will see that all trees are either fruitful, or some on which there is no likeness of seed [?], other trees like these,
which have no fruit, as is supposed.
And each of them has seed, that grain which is at the back of the leaf, the tree [?],
which, planted from a branch, puts forth roots; and perhaps within the roots that are planted is the power of seed.
But, as we said, those trees were made worthy of mention which [?] of ours, from whose fruits food is prepared for people.
The vine brings forth wine, by which the heart of man rejoices; and the olive produces fruit

which is able to gladden the face. For this reason the root of the vine came forth swiftly from nature, and around it its tender branches spread out upon the ground, and its shoot and tendril [?] and unripe grape and cluster, the sight.
That of the vine [?], understand, and even unwillingly you will recall that parable of the Lord, which [says] that:

"He is the vine and my Father the worker"; and each of us who has been planted by faith in the Church he called a branch, and he asks fruit of us, so that he may not reproach our idleness and give us over to the fire.
And he often likens the souls of men to a vineyard, saying:

"A vineyard came to be, grape-bearing [?], on a fertile horn of land." And again: "I planted a vineyard and enclosed it with a fence": those around whom he set as a fence the commandments of God [and the guard?] of the angels, as it is said:
"The camp of the angels of the Lord surrounds those who fear him," and again, that:

"He planted them in the Church like pillars: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers." He raises [?] our thought by the likeness of all of them, and did not leave them on the ground to be trampled underfoot.
And he wishes us to entwine ourselves in love of our neighbor, like the tendrils of the vine, and to take our rest with him,
so that our movement may always be upward, as, for example, Babylon [?] high above us, so that we might take upon ourselves the digging.

And the digging of the soul is the casting off of the cares of the world, fleshly love, the desire for possessions, and the pursuit of that loathsome glory; and it is at rest and has cast off from itself

The heaviness of the earth of thought [?] — everything ought to be done according to the proverbs of Solomon, so that no one grows bold [?]; that is, let no one hunt for praise from outsiders through human virtues. And let the fruit of that true husbandman be his own, in his own storehouses.
And be like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God. You will be stripped [?] of hope, but be for your own [?] by faith.

And in this you will resemble the fruitfulness of the olive tree, and in this imitate it and act. And let us turn back again to examine those wisely fashioned works: how many there are, and some are unfruitful,
and some are for use in ships and some for burning! And again, every tree has great arrangement in its own parts,
and it is hard to find the distinctive character of each of them and to observe their many varieties.
how some of them are deep-rooted and some are not;

And why are some straight-grown and single-branched, and some low, with their branches spreading out? How is it that those which are tall and many-branched have their roots in the depth, and around those roots are small roots,
made by nature in the likeness of a foundation,
so that they may bear its weight? How many are the kinds of bark of trees! For in bark [?], and some are rough, and some have one bark and some many.
And this is wonderful: that they resemble, in their own way, human youth and old age.
For the bark of the young ones is smooth and taut, while the bark of the aged dries out and becomes rough.
And some, when their root sprouts again [?], as though it had died by that cutting.

and the oak, when it is cut down or burned, its root sprouts up again and it becomes a grove of tall trees [?]. And we see many trees that are healed by farmers of the badness of their nature, as for example the sour pomegranate and the bitter almond.
For they bore through their root and insert into its pith a wedge of [?] (perhaps pine), and they are changed into goodness and bring forth good fruit. Likewise,
if anyone is in evil,
let him not despair of life, since it is known [?] that for the soul [care?] drives out many diseases. A difference which no one is able to recount.
For the variety of trees divides even a single kind of fruit tree into male and female,
And among date palms they distinguish the male and the female.

And sometimes you would see the female palms, [?], which desire to join with the male; and you would see the tree-healers, how they put the issue of the male palm into the female in the manner of seed, and it is as if it perceived some taste of it, and it gathers its branches up again in its former shape. And they say the same also of the fig. And for this reason they plant the wild fig beside the garden fig.
And certain others, when they see a garden fig shedding its fruit, take some of the fruit of the wild one and hang it on the tree, and from then on it no longer sheds its fruit.
Why do you think this behavior exists in nature? So that we might imitate those who are outside the Law in the vigor of their good works.
When you see in this life someone from among the pagans,
or from among the heretics, who are [?] of the church, in good order of conduct,

Hasten to make progress in this, and be like the fruitful fig, which through its nearness to the wild fig [?] no longer sheds [its fruit]. And this is the distinction of the nature of trees, a little out of much that could be said. But who could recount the multitude of their fruits, or their shape and their colour, or the particular quality of their taste, or the usefulness of each of them?!

How do some ripen naked in the sun, and some within a sheath, filling out under a covering [?]? And why is the fruit of some tender while the leaf is thick, and of others the fruit is hard while the leaf is thin, as for example the walnut? For the former, because of its weakness, needed great help, while for the latter the thickness of the leaf would have been harmful because of its shade.

For the leaf of the vine is such [?] that the cluster may be protected from harm from the air and may receive the blaze of the sun through the thinness of the leaf. Nothing is without cause, and nothing is at random; everything is inexpressible [?].
What human mind can reach so far as to see clearly the property and distinction of each of them, and to tell [?] the hidden causes? From a single water the root draws,
and it nourishes the roots in one way, the bark in another, the branches in another, the wood in another, and the inner heart in another.
And from that nourishment come the leaf, the tips and the branches, and it gives richness to the fruit;

and the resin of trees and their milky sap come forth from the same sun and the same cause, [?] which resin cannot reach, and another [?] of the balsam in Egypt and Libya. And they say that amber congeals [?] in water and becomes like [?], and to this statement the fine particles and tiny creatures that stick to it bear witness,
while it is still fresh, and they remain inside it.
And who, not knowing by experience that distinction among resins, [could say] what manner of thing it is that there is wine in the vine and oil in the olive?
And not only that there is so much sweetness, found [?] in it, but even among sweet fruits there is much distinction.
The sweetness that is in the vine is one thing, that in the apple another, and that in the fig and the date another.
And again I wish that you would be an investigator, with love of wisdom, of how water itself is soft to the senses in these, and sometimes bites the palate
when it turns sour in other trees;
and again sometimes it offends the senses when it turns to bitterness and becomes so in wormwood and scammony, and when it comes to be in the acorn and the chestnut,
[?]; in the [?] and the walnut it is changed into the nature of oil? And why do I speak of distant things, when in a single fig many qualities arise?
For it is bitter in the sap and sweet in the fruit;
and again, in the vine it is astringent in the shoots and sweet in the clusters.
And in the distinction of colors! How it appears in the garden: in this one red, and in this one violet,
and in this one white; and even more than these colors, the multitude of its various fragrances.
