And the inquiry will become excessive unless I restrain and compel [myself] to go along with [?] created things; the day would surely come to an end
while I am revealing to you the great wisdom of God from these small words: "Let the earth bring forth the fruitful tree, bearing fruit upon the earth."
And at once the tops of the mountains were clothed, and the gardens were made ready, and the riverbanks were adorned with a multitude of trees: some to adorn human tables,
and some to provide pasture for animals from their leaves and fruits. From them come for us the means and benefit of healing: the juice of meadow plants, gums, branches, barks, seeds, and everything,
that has been discovered through long experience, which we encountered through particular instances [?], and from which we selected what was beneficial.
And [?] and waterless, flowering and flowerless: from what is small, know what is great, and add to your wonder and increase your love of the Creator.

And consider how he created some trees always adorned with foliage and others that become bare; and of those adorned with foliage, some shed their leaves, and some are always [?] so, for example the olive and the pine,
for although their leaves fall, they do not become bare and are always leafy.
But the date palm is always leafy,
for its leaf never falls at all. Look again: it is counted among the water-loving trees, and yet it is also found in desert places.
For this reason Jeremiah [?] a two-sided nature. "Let the earth bring forth," he says.
This small command at once became a great nature, and the prepared word, swifter than our thought, made many trees, each with its own particular character.
That same command, even until now, urges the earth at every turning of the year to bring forth the power it has for producing grass, seeds and trees.

Just as a spinning top is first given a blow, and even until now remains in that same motion: when it has fixed its point, it spins around itself. So too is the succession: as it received the first command, so it proceeds in the times to come, until it reaches the end of all things. Toward that end let us all hasten, fruitful and full of good works, so that we may be planted in the house of the Lord;
flourishing in the courts of the house of our God, [?] our [?], whose is the glory and the power unto the ages of ages,
Amen.
Lines: 573.

Spoken by the same: Chapter Six. Whoever watches a contestant ought to have courage himself. And this is known from the rules of the games, for those who preside over the arena command that no one be found with his head covered in the arena.
He wants this so that those who sit there are not only spectators but also fellow contestants. In the same way it is right for the one
who investigates very great matters and hears unspeakable wisdom to have the means to understand what is set before him. Let him share the contest with me as far as his strength allows,
so that he will not be a judge beside me,
but as a contestant, lest perhaps he fail to sow with me [?] and become harmful [?]; for we have come to the inquiry into the creation of the world and the knowledge of it, of this world.
But from whom [?] his servant, and he spoke to him face to face and not in parables; and he is compelled, so that his mind may not be veiled for the inquiry into this matter set before us.
If on a clear night you have seen the indescribable beauty of the stars, you have thought about the Maker of all things, and asked who it was that painted the heavens with such flowers,

and how the wonders of the day are, [?] to their eyes, with a wakeful mind, from these visible things to the invisible one. If you are like this, have you not come as a well-prepared hearer, worthy of that blessed theater?
Come, then, and I will lead you into the hidden wonders of the city, as one leads someone into a city unknown to him.
This is the city that was our dwelling, from which the man-slaying devil made us strangers, and by his deception he took captive the people in it.
And you will see the first creation of man, and the death that overtook us, which was planted by sin, by the devil, that evil beginning,
so that you may know that by nature he is of the earth, and that man, by God's [?], is a ruler established over the beasts and over soulless things.
[?] is he in the treasures of nature, who is able to climb up to heaven through the wealth of his thought. If we understand this,
we will be able to know ourselves as well, and to know God our Creator. We will serve him and minister to our Lord and glorify the Father,
our nurturer, and we will love the Son, from the guide [?] of our life, of the living soul [?], in this life and in the one to come.

And let us not cease from serving him who has granted us [?]; may he fulfill for us what was promised and confirm for us that in which we hope. And if this present age is like this, what then will that age to come be like? If the greatness of heaven
is exalted above human thought, what mind, then, is able to search out that beginningless nature? If this sun, which is below, is so beautiful and so great in its course through all things,
so that its measure does not exceed all this distance of the way [?], it is

like an eye among created things. If we cannot be satiated with the sight of it, how then shall we be satiated with the beauty of that Sun of Righteousness? If a blind man feels deprivation [?], will he be deprived of the true one [?]?
"And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to illuminate the earth and to divide between the day and the night." Heaven and earth came first.
And of this [?], both day and night. And it came to be, and the dry land appeared;
And the water gathered into a fixed, standing gathering-place; the earth brought forth the fruit of plants.
and there was not yet a sun, nor a moon. This was so that you would not say, as the godless do, that the sun is the creator of plants.
For this reason the fourth day came about. And then God said: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven." When you have recognized the one who speaks, join the hearer to him at once.
God said: "Let there be luminaries," and God made the luminaries. Are there two persons in this?

In all of this that is said, the word concerning theology is secretly sown. And the use of the luminaries' being is that they may be luminaries of the earth. And if someone should say, "The [nature] of light existed first; why is it said that the sun became an illuminator of the earth?", let us answer him: "Do not mock the ignorance of our speech,
for we do not follow [?]; there are not among us snatchers at words and seekers after beauty of sounds, and in every place we choose the truth of the words."
And know that he has clearly revealed what he intended. And he said "illumination" in place of "light."
And this does not contradict what was said about the light. For at that time [?] was created, and now this body of the sun came into being,

so that this light may be [?]: it is one thing, and a lamp and light would be [?]. And those luminaries were made of [?] that fine [substance] in which there is no density. Just as the Apostle names certain people luminaries of the world, the true [light] of the world is another, by which the saints became lamps in the Spirit,
whom they were teaching and delivering from that darkness. And likewise the Creator of all this created this sun, and set it upon that light, and kindled it in the world like a lamp.
And let no one deny what has been said, that the radiance of the light is one thing, and the body that lies within the light is another.

For in all firebrands [?] one distinguishes the receiver and the quality that falls upon it. And just as whiteness in nature [?], what is now said is by the mind opposed one to the other, and is mingled by the power of the Creator. And do not tell me any longer that it is impossible to separate these from one another.
Nor do I tell you that you and I are able to separate the light from the body of the sun,
but what is separated by our reasoning is easily done in actual fact by its Creator.
And you are not able to separate the power of burning fire [?]; by an astonishing sight he willed the turning of his servant,
and he made in that bramble a fire that only gave light, without burning power,
as the Psalm testifies, saying: "The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire." Therefore the mystery spoken of teaches us

that at that time, at the recompense of deeds, its light will be separated [?] to be the delight of the saints, and its painful burning will be set apart as torment for the punishment of sinners. And again, from what the moon undergoes we are able to find the truth: its whole body is not consumed,
but the light that is in it withdraws, and it seems to us that it is being added to [?] they appear in it [?]. They testify that its body is not destroyed.
For you can easily see this when the air is clear, when its disc is without light: just as you see it from its one part, you may see the other part that is unlit.
and do not think that the light of the moon has entered it as moonlight [?] from another source, since when it draws near the sun,

its light diminishes, and when it moves away, on day three [?] to investigate this [?]; but I declare that its body is one thing, and that which illuminates it is so blended in it and does not depart from it.
But as for the moon, insofar as it points to the truth [?], these too were commanded to divide between day and night.
And above it was said that God divided between light and darkness, for at that time he made their natures separate, so that they would have no fellowship with one another,
Light is with darkness and darkness with light; that shadow becomes darkness,
when light is covered by some body. In the morning it stretches out toward the west, in the evening it bends toward the east, [?] it is seen. From the earth comes the nature of night.
And this is what was meant by the saying that God divided between the light and between the darkness,

For darkness flees from light, and the sun was given command over their opposition to each other, so that it should rule when the disk is filled and the two [?] sun, and the moon goes down into a dark place,
and when the sun rises, sometimes it [the moon] can be seen, if the moon's light is not complete in its shape at night.

This does not overturn what was said. When the moon is full, it has authority over the night. It surpasses the stars in brightness and lights the whole earth evenly. "And let them be for signs." The signs of the lights are useful for human life, as long as no one goes beyond measure in investigation. From them one may learn the [?] of the winds, which is shown by the sun and by the appearances of the sun.

In this way you will see what is going to happen. When the sky is overcast and its glow is red, its color appears red and like embers, and the thickness of the air produces this kind of sight for the eyes.
And when the still air is not dispersed by the blaze of the sun, it foretells
that an abundance of vapor from the earth [?] in the air, and has brought rain to those places in which it gathers.

And likewise again the moon and the sun, when there stands around it what are called "shetsvani" [halos?], foretell very great rains. And again what is called the anthelion, when it gathers on the course of the sun, is a sign of disturbances of the air.
And in the clouds, the colors of the bow in the upper part foretell heavy rains or a violent change of the air.
And again many signs become known to those who inquire, from the waning of the moon and from its fullness, for the air of the earth changes together with the change of its shapes.
For when it appears pure by day, it foretells purity of the air; and when something of it is seen reddish, [?] or a violent rush of south wind.
And who does not know [?] from these things?
And what is going to come from the violence of the wind, so that one may keep his ship in harbor and be saved; and it is possible for those traveling on the road [?] from the air,
when those who take care of the field and of the planting of trees [?]. Hence the Lord has said that the passing away of this world will come about from signs of the sun and moon and stars.
For the sun will be turned into blood and the moon will not give its light: these are words of the end of the world.
But those who go beyond the [?] drag what has been said over to the birth of man, [saying that] our life is joined to the movement of the stars,
and for this reason the Chaldeans suppose that the causes of the things that befall us come from the stars.

And the word of Scripture, which says plainly, "Let them be for signs," they did not understand, that it was said concerning the turning of the seasons and the change of the air. Instead they say, "These stars of this tower [?] are for manifold lives.

And they bring one another into conjunction, and from them comes such and such a birth; and when they move in another way, they produce something contrary to this." And perhaps it is not useless for us
to show briefly and speak a word that not only is [?], but is drawn from what was said by them themselves, against them,
Those who had been caught in their error,

and their snare [?] had been caught in such a thing. These are the ones who invented the doctrine of nativities. For this reason, when they realized that they erred greatly over long spans of time, they shortened the [?] of the times very much, down to even a small [interval],

the one the Apostle mentioned, "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye." In it the nativity of those being born is divided. And they say that the one born in this moment will be master over cities and ruler over troops, a seizer of riches.
and the one born in the next instant is a beggar from door to door for his daily food. For this reason its circle was divided into twelve parts in that immovable sphere,
each of thirty days. For this reason they divided each of those twelve into thirty parts, and each part of those thirty they divided into sixty,
and each of those sixty they divided again into sixty parts.
Let us now bring forward the nativity of those born and see
whether they are able to attain the exact division of this time.

When a child is born, [?] whether the child is a girl or a boy [?], and she still waits for the crying of the newborn; at that time [?] of those minute parts [pass]. As you please, how many pass before the word of the one who reports it? And after this the observer of the hour may be found standing outside that house
in which the newborn was born, [to note] which star is rising and whether it is of the day or of the night.
How great a number of those sixtieths [passes] in that time? For [it is necessary to find] not only the natural indicator of the hour,
but from the parts of its parts and from the parts of that sixtieth it is necessary to find, in each of the seven
wandering stars, what the kinship and the aspect toward one another were at the birth of that person, [so they say,] and these are to be known in truth;
and in this lies the error and folly of their whole enterprise. Now therefore those are laughable who [?], even those who suppose that there is knowledge in their enterprise.
And see again how they judge! They say that a certain person is long-haired and has beautiful eyes,

"and this," they say, "is because his birth was in the Ram, and this animal is known by these things." And again, the same person is great-souled, because the ram is a leader. And again he is acquisitive, because the ram sheds its wool without labor and then puts on another coat.
And another was born in the Bull, so he is laborious and servile, since this animal is likewise under the yoke.
And this one was born in the Scorpion, a biter, and he resembles that animal; for he is of justice [?], like the balance that is among men, they say. And who is as worthy of mockery as these!
The Ram, in which you placed the birth of a man, is one of those twelve parts of the heaven, in which, when the sun has come round to it, the beginning of spring occurs.
And the Scales and the Bull likewise are each one of those twelve,

which are in the circle of those animals. You say that the beginning of the causes of the life of those born comes from there, and after that you liken their minds to those animals and to the grazing beasts among us?
And you say that the one born in the Ram is generous, [?] that sheep of the heavens is of this nature.
O speaker, how do you say that birth, so that you might convince us of it, [?] of the minds then? And if this statement is laughable, he is worse who wants what is impossible.
But this wisdom of theirs is like a spider's web. When a gnat or an insect, or some other of such weak creatures, comes near it, it touches it and is caught;
and when one of the strong creatures touches it, it tears it apart and destroys it.

And they say not only this, but also the deeds that are under our power, which we do by our own will, both good and evil: they have ascribed the causes of these to the stars. And therefore their opposition is laughable; but lest many fall into that error of theirs, it is not right for us to keep silent.
And first of all let us ask them this: does not the configuration of the stars change every day, with a very great change?
For the stars that are called wandering are always moving,
and some of them meet their companion quickly and some more slowly, and sometimes they are hidden.
And as you say, the sighting of a beneficent star has power over a birth.
And sometimes, through their error, they do not find the moment at which the beneficent star is recognized for one of the infants, and he is recorded as evil.
And in such reasoning there is great foolishness and, still more, godlessness.
For those harmful stars ascribe their evil to their Creator. For if their evil is by nature, [?] is [?] of evil?!

And if the evil is by their will, then are they indeed living beings that have a will and move by their own authority?! And this lie about soulless things exceeds all madness. And again, why do they not say that every star has evil and good according to its dominion, that when it is in this place, and they have seen it favorably from another star, it is harmful,
and when it turns aside a little,
it passes out? And if at every blink of an eye, within the hours, they change their configuration, and within them in a day there is the birth of kings,
then why are kings not born every day? Or why do kings not have an inheritance?
And does none of the kings know from the stars the kingship of his son? For no human being has such authority.
And how did Uzziah beget Jotham, and Jotham beget Ahaz, and Ahaz beget Hezekiah?

And not even one hour of servitude came upon them. And again, if the beginning of good and evil is not from us, but is laid upon us involuntarily from birth itself, then he lied who said that good and evil are from us;
and judges are indeed superfluous, since they praise the good and condemn the evil.

And if punishment is due for that theft, [?] nor to that man for murder; for even if he had wanted to restrain his hand, he could not have done so because of the compulsion that made him act involuntarily.
And again, craftsmen labor in vain. And farmers will surely become fruitful, and again the merchant will surely become rich,
even if he does not want wealth, since that decree,
which is upon him, and hope, since righteousness would not be honored nor sin punished, nor would these have come about by the will of men.
And if anything happens by the compulsion of the stars, then surely there is no justice of God by which he would repay anyone according to his deeds; and this belongs properly to God alone.
And this is enough for us by way of reply to them, for you, you [?] are alive in soul; and at this time it is not opportune to speak the rest of the discourse against them:
Let them be signs and wonders of seasons and of days and of years.
We have spoken; but concerning seasons we say that they are the divisions of the year: winter and spring, summer and autumn,
which come about in due order in the course of the luminaries.
And winter occurs when the sun turns toward the south, and the shadow of night becomes great over the earth among us;
and the air that is over the earth grows cold, and all the moist vapors gather around us, and they are the cause of rain and of an abundance of snows.
And again, when it rises from the southern parts, it comes to the middle and makes days and nights equal;
and as far as it brings about the equalization,

spring also comes about, which is the beginning of the sprouting of every plant, and the giver of life to most trees, and the preserver of the kind of the living creatures of land and of water, and the continuer of births.

And then from there the sun moves and goes toward the north and brings about the length of the days and dries all the earth, and by this it also helps the ripening of the fields; at every season, by the shortness of the shadow and by its height above the earth, it illumines the places in which we are.
For in these days it is short, and in short days the shade is long.
And this is shown among us, whose shadow is single, who dwell in that northern land.
And there are other places which at midday to the south [?]. For it shines and reaches into pits with narrow mouths and illumines them.

Therefore they are called "shadowless." But those who live beyond the land of the fragrant spices have their shadow falling on both sides. In this region only their shadow reaches at the [?] of the days. Therefore they are called "two-shadowed." All this happens
when the sun turns toward the north. From these things we may consider how quickly the air is burned by the sun, and the many effects that come from it.
And then the season of spring comes upon us,
and it greatly lessens the heat of the air, and little by little it passes from warmth to a temperate measure.
and it brings us forward into winter without hardship, because when it begins to incline from the north toward the south.
This division of the seasons follows the course [?] of the sun and governs our life.
It says, "Let them be for days." This does not mean that they make the days, but that they have authority over the days. For day and night came into being before these luminaries.
As the Psalm teaches, saying: "He made the sun to rule the day, and the moon and stars to rule the night." The authority of the day?
For it carries the light, and when it rises; and if anyone should say,
that the definition of day is air illuminated by the sun, and day is the measure of time
during which the sun is above the earth. And the sun and the moon were made for years.
When the moon has completed its course twelve times, that is one year. And at times a month of the seasons is inserted, as they did at first, and the pagans who were before them.

The solar year is [when] it comes to the same place. [?] "And God made the great lights." For the word "great" is used absolutely, as the earth is great, and [relatively, as] a horse is great and an ox is great, not because of the size of their stature,
but [because of] this greatness of others [?]. Is it so here?
Do we then speak of the greatness of the lights as when we have compared it with something smaller than it?
Or shall we speak of it as belonging to their nature? But I say that they were not called great for this reason,
that they are larger than the other stars, but they were called great for this reason,
that there is in their light enough to illuminate the sky and the earth and the air and the sea.
And when they are in any part of the sky, in the east or in the west or in the middle, they [?] for people alike on every side.
And this is the true proof of their greatness, that the expanse of the earth does not cause them to appear larger or smaller.
For something far from us we see as small, and when we approach it, its size becomes evident.
But no one comes closer to the sun or moves farther from it; rather it is seen equally from every side.
And this is known from the fact that Indians and Britons see it alike.

So it does not appear small to those in the east when it reaches the west, nor does it appear small to those in the west when it rises, nor, when it is in the very middle of the sky, does it change for those who see it from either side.
And do not let this appearance deceive you, nor, because the sun looks only a cubit across, should you suppose that to be its size.
For at a great distance of space the power of the organs of sight fails in the air and is diminished, and it cannot reach a far-off place.
And since our sight is small, it sees everything as small.
But seeing is deceptive, and the instrument that judges is not trustworthy. Recall what happens to you, and learn by yourself the truth of this statement.
For at some time you have been on the top of a mountain, and there the ploughing teams and ploughmen [appeared] like ants.
And when you look from a high [?] place toward the sea, you see great islands, and great ships under way that are smaller than a dove.
For sight is dispersed in the air, as we said, and becomes too weak to see each thing as it is.
And great wooded mountains you see as round and smooth, for the eye reaches only the ridge of the mountain, and because of its weakness it cannot see its ravines.
Likewise it does not recognize the shapes of bodies, but takes four-walled towers to be round.
And in many ways you may learn that the eye does not truly see anything in distant places.

Now then, that luminary is great, as Scripture has testified, and greater than what is visible of it by many times beyond counting. And let this too serve as information for you: that the stars which are in the heavens are many and countless, and all the light that is gathered from them
cannot dispel the darkness of the night.
But this one alone, when it is above the covering [of the earth], and even more before it has yet shone forth upon the earth, destroys that darkness.
And its light surpasses the stars, and it breaks up and melts this cold and frozen air over the earth.

For this reason dews and breezes flow over the earth when the morning is clear. And if its light did not come forth from a great disk, how could it illuminate this great earth in a single twinkling of an eye?

And observe here the wisdom of the Creator, how he gave it heat according to the measure of his wisdom, so that it would not burn up the earth by an excess of its heat, nor would the earth remain cold and unfruitful through a deficiency of heat.
And the same is known concerning the moon. For after the sun its body is great and bright.

But its size is not always visible; rather, sometimes it appears full in its circle and sometimes deficient, and its waning occurs on both of its sides: on one side it decreases and on the other side it increases.
And when it decreases above, it increases below, and sometimes it decreases below and increases above.
And there is a mysterious lesson of the Creator's wisdom in the changing of its shapes, so that it may be for us a true image in our nature,
for nothing among human affairs is stable, but some of them attain completion from nothing, and others, once they have attained it, then vanish.

Now then, by observing the moon, let us understand the conditions of our own nature. When we consider how quickly human affairs pass away, let us not count the joy of this life as blessed. Let us not put our hope in unstable wealth. Let us despise the perishable flesh and take care of the soul.
whose waning little by little distresses you; let this distress you even more, when the soul has acquired virtue
and loses it through negligence, and does not stay steady in one course but is changed into another mind. And truly, as Scripture has said, the fool changes as the moon does. And it seems to me
that the minds of living creatures and whatever else springs up from the earth are greatly changed by the change of the moon.

For bodies change with the moon's fullness just as they do with its waning. When the moon wanes, bodies become empty. When it is completed in fullness, those bodies too are completed and filled, for it brings moisture mixed with heat.

And this is evident from those who sleep under the moon and from raw meat on which the moon has shone, for it quickly becomes moist and spoils; and also from the brains of animals, and the moist creatures of the sea, and the hearts of trees.
And it would not have reached so as to change all these things if it were not great in power, both it and the causes
that occur in the air, which come about through the changes of the moon,

This is evident, just as the movement of the air at once, and the movement of the flow of the water of the Ocean, [?] the moon's movement, as those who live by it have said. And the straits flow according to the form of the moon,
but only at the birth of the moon do they flow unceasingly, until the moon appears, and then the water turns back again according to its own swell [?].

And the western sea sometimes increases the swell [?] of its waters and overflows, and sometimes it subsides and stands back in retreat, as if it were being drawn in and then sent out again by those same winds.
I have said this to make known the greatness of the luminaries, and to prove that not one letter of the divine books is in vain,

although this speech of mine has not attained to it, and there would still be room for much discourse about the size of the sun and moon and the distance of their expanses [?], from those who investigate in minute detail the power of their workings. But with goodness of mind it is proper
that we should blame our own weakness,
so that we may not measure the greatness of God's creatures by our words, but may understand from the little that has been said how many things have gone unmentioned.
And again, do not measure the matters of the moon with the eye, but with reason, which is nearer to finding the truth. For it is said that the moon is brought down by some contrivance.
What sorcery of magicians is able to shake that which he himself established?
And if someone were to bring it down, what place could contain it? And if you wish to learn the size of the moon from small examples,
the cities that are throughout the whole world, however far apart from one another, receive the light of the moon equally, as the narrow streets facing east receive it.
And if it were not face to face with them all, it would surely not shine on them equally; rather, the narrow streets before its face would be lit like broad streets.

And its light would rather be hidden from those on this side and on that. For example, when there is a lamp in a house, and people stand around it, the shadow of the one standing before it stretches out straight, and the shadows of the others on this side and on that.
And if the light of the moon were not great, it would not reach equally in every direction.
And those who dwell in the east and in the west, and those toward the north, and the inhabitants of the deep and scorching south, all attain to its light, wherever it shines forth.
Over all these, the great and even expanse shows the greatness of the moon.
And this is enough to say about the size of the sun and moon.
And may he who has granted us understanding, so that from small creatures we may know the greatness of the Creator's wisdom, grant us great reflection from the great ones also,
by which we may know our Creator, even though, when the sun and moon are compared with him, they are found to be like ants and gnats.
And the greatness of the God of all cannot be compared with the greatness of these,
but by a small and worthless likeness let us rise up to him, just as we arrive at knowledge of him through the least grass and animal. And let what has been said be enough.
And I give thanks to God, who has granted me the ministry of these words, and you too give thanks to him who nourishes you with spiritual food.

And he who [?] has nourished you with barley bread from our contemptible voice. And may he nourish you fully according to your faith, and grant you the revelation of the Holy Spirit through Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory to the ages of ages, amen.
Lines: 770.
Discourse of the same, chapter seven. "And God said: Let the waters bring forth creeping living things according to their kinds,
and winged birds in the firmament of heaven according to their kinds." After the creation of the luminaries the waters were filled with creeping living things, so that these too might be adorned.
For the earth had been adorned with plants, and the heaven had received the flower of the stars and had been adorned with those two great luminaries, as if with eyes;
only the realm of the waters remained, that its beauty might be given to it.
The command came, and the rivers became possessors and the lakes bearers, each of them of the kinds that belong to its nature;
and the sea was in labor with all the creeping things of the water. And nothing that was in the lakes and marshes remained idle in it, without a share in creation.
But frogs and gnats came forth from them, for what is visible now teaches us about what happened then.

Thus all hastened to the service of their Creator, and those whose multitude of kinds no one is able to recount, the great power of God immediately showed to be alive, existing and moving; by his ineffable command the power of life came into being in the waters.

Let the waters bring forth creeping living things. Now the first ensouled living being was created, which has sensation. Although it is said of plants and trees that they have the power of increase and growth, yet they are neither living nor ensouled. For this reason the waters bring forth creeping things. Every swimmer, which swims on the surface of the water and cleaves the depths, is of the nature of creeping things. And if there are some water creatures that are many [?], most of them are amphibious, such as the tortoise and [?], and the river-horse, and frogs, and crabs. Yet these [?] are first of all swimmers. For this reason the waters bring forth creeping things.
By this small word, which of created things was not made: those that bear live young, such as seals and dolphins and torpedo rays and those like them, which are called selachians,
and the egg-laying kinds, which are the majority of fish, scaly and scaleless, finned and finless?
The voice of the command is small; or rather it is not even a voice, but only an instant and an impulse of the will,
yet the fruitfulness of the command is equal to the number of the fishes' combinations and divisions,
for counting the waves, or measuring the waters of the sea with a cup, is easier than counting them.

Let the waters bring forth creeping things of ensouled living beings. In these were born the fish of the abyss and of the seashore, of the depths and of the rocks, those that go in shoals and those that go alone, sea monsters, and huge and tiny fish.
By that same command and by that same power both the small and the great came to be. Let the waters bring forth.
He has shown you the kinship of swimming creatures with the waters; for this reason, when a fish comes out of the water, it dies in this air.
And just as the life of land creatures comes from the air, so too the life of swimming creatures comes from the waters.
And the reason for this is evident: for our lung is a thin organ, and by inhaling through the throat it takes in air and cools the heat that is within us,
but fish, by opening and closing their gills, take in water and let it out; and this is their organ of breathing. And fish have a separate portion, a separate nature, and separate food.
For this reason they cannot live with humans, nor do they endure the touch of a human hand. "Let the waters bring forth creeping living things, kind by kind."

He commanded the beginning of every kind, so that within nature there might be a likeness of kind, but he left their multiplication to come about by birth, when increase and multiplication should be ordained for them. Of another kind are the shelled creatures, such as the conch [?],
and the comb-shell, and the sea spoon, and many other varieties of this sort.
And of another kind again are those called soft-shelled, such as crabs and the crayfish; and those called soft,
whose flesh is soft and loose, such as the cuttlefish and the many-footed octopus and those like them. And again among these there are many divisions, as for example:
the snake-fish and the sea monsters and the moray, in rivers and [?] and lakes, which by nature resemble biting creatures more
than fish. Of another kind again are those that lay eggs, and of another, those that give birth.
Those that give birth to live young are the ones called selachians, for example sea-dogs, dolphins and seals,

of which it is said that they swallow their own young when they are afraid of another animal, and when the danger has passed, they bring them out again. "Let the waters bring forth creeping things, each according to its kind." The great sea creatures are of one kind and the small fishes of another,
and again among the fish, too, there is much division, separated kind by kind, both in name and in food,
and in form, and in size and in the condition of their flesh, and they differ from one another. And they are of many different colors.
Who are those who search out their beings and their divisions? For they say that they live in many shoals, and they report their number;
has anyone grown old on the seashore so as to give a true account of them?
The hunters of the Indian sea tell us of some, and those who hunt in the sea of Egypt of others, and the islanders of others.
And all of them, small and great, were brought forth by that command and that inexpressible power.
How many are theirs, and how many of what is theirs! Many of the kinds do not lay eggs as hens do, nor do they build a nest,
nor do they rear their young with labor, but when one of them lays an egg, that egg falls into the water and comes alive.
And the generation of every race among them is unmixed with another nature, and [?] of the birds are among the fish,
which might have obtained what it needs incompletely in its teeth, as for example the ox and the sheep. And there is none among them that chews the cud, except the scarus alone, as some say.
And all fish have sharp teeth set in them, so that food does not fall out during their constant chewing, and if they did not chew it quickly and take it down into the belly,
the water would scatter it and carry that food away.
And the food of some fish is one thing, and that of others is another: [?].
And whichever one is large eats the small.
And sometimes a fish swallows one smaller than itself; it swallows it [?],

and both of them come to be [?]. And in the same way we men act, by our persecution, toward those weaker than ourselves. What difference is there between that last fish and the lover of wealth, who in his greed hides [?] in the bosoms of his avarice? He took a vessel [?] for you.
And you have become more unjust than the greedy man. See that your end is not like that of the fish, and that a hook [?] or a net does not come upon you.
For we too will not escape eternal punishment if we cling to injustice. And when you have learned the cunning among feeble animals
and their deceit, I wish that, when you remember them, you keep away [?] is in its shell, and hunting it out of its shells is difficult for it.
For nature [?] for it a hard covering, for the sake of the tenderness of its flesh. For this reason it is called 'hide-shelled'.

And as those shells close tightly, the crab's claws remain useless. And when it sees that creature laid open, warming itself in the heat under the sun, it throws a small pebble [?] into that shell, so that it can no longer close its shells against the crab. It accomplishes this by its stratagem [?] is the contrivance
which have no voice
and no speech! And I want from you that [?] for the sake of gain [?], and that you stop doing evil to your neighbour.
And such is the one who goes to his neighbor with guile and seeks an opportune moment [at the expense] of another. And flee from imitating the wicked, and let your own possessions be enough for you.
For poverty with righteousness is more excellent among the prudent. I will not forget the cunning and the theft of the octopus, which takes on the color of every rock to which it clings.
For when a fish swims around that rock, it rushes upon it unperceived, and that fish becomes ready prey for that cunning one. [?] they follow rulers,
who never stay fixed on any one thing, but are changeable. They honor purity with the pure and commit adultery with adulterers,
and they change according to the will of everyone.
From these it is difficult to get away, and to guard against the harm they do.
For their evil is deep and hidden by their love. And the Lord called such as these ravening wolves,
who appear in sheep's clothing. [?] from that evil of the octopuses, and pursue righteousness and innocence and simplicity.

The serpent is cunning and the righteous man is simple, like Jacob. The Lord settles those of one manner in a house. This sea [?]: all the creeping things without number, small living creatures together with large ones; their creation is with wisdom and good order.
And it is not only that we do not think [?] the fish, but there is something among them that it is also right to imitate.
Namely, that the kinds of fish have divided their dwellings among one another, but they stay within their own boundaries.
And there is no surveyor among them who might have measured out their dwelling place. Nor are they divided by boundary and wall, but straightaway what is its own was appointed for each of them.
In this gulf some fish graze, and in other gulfs they graze [?].
And it is not that the height of mountains keeps them from going to one another,
but the law of nature apportions to each of them what benefits it, equally and with justice.
But we are not so; rather, we cross the boundary that our fathers set, we join houses to our house, to our fields [?],

and those of our own [?] the sea that lies outside the inhabited places, in which there are no islands, which has no land beyond it to cross over to, but it is stagnant [?], and sailors do not travel on it, neither for need nor for sightseeing.
There are huge sea monsters there, which resemble huge mountains, remaining within those boundaries and not [?] the islands.
And thus every kind of fish is divided among the regions of the sea's depth for itself, as if they were cities and villages or ancient homelands.
And some fish are migratory.
As if by a single resolve, they all alike move to another territory when the time of their spawning arrives,
some going off through other parts of the sea and some to other parts, and they arrive; you may see [?] their coming up, as it were, waves one following after another,
and they go from the sea to the Euxine Sea. By the command of what king,
or what written decree was read out to the people, that could have appointed that time for them?!
Behold, you see the divine command filling all things and reaching from the great [?]; the fish does not transgress the law of nature,
and we human beings do not submit to the teaching of our Savior. You [?] the fish, which has not even speech, but be afraid,
so that you may not be more brutish than it. Only listen to the fish: does it not give voice by its deeds, when it sets out on a far journey for the preservation of its kind?
They have no speech, but they have among them [?]:
"Let us go to the northern sea." For the water of that deep is sweeter than that of other seas; the sun lingers only a little over it and does not greatly [?] the sweetness of the water.
And for this reason they sometimes swim in rivers, outside the sea, as more suitable for rearing.
And when what they intended has been accomplished, they return all together to their own dwelling, they say.

With breathing [?] they say that the northern sea is spread out flat on the surface [?], and there are few deep hollows in it; the winds stir it up from the bottom, until the sand of the abyss is mixed up with the waves.
And moreover it is cold in winter time, for many very great rivers flow into it.
And since we have enjoyed it during summer time as much as was fitting, again in winter [?] let us go to the warmth of the deep and to those sunny places, from the calm places [?]."
I saw this and marveled at the wisdom of God in all things. If brute beasts toil for their own life,
and fish know what is profitable to them and what is harmful, what then shall we say, we who are honored with reason,
and instructed in the Law, directed by the promise, made wise by the Spirit, who manage our affairs worse than the brute fish?
For it is able [?], and we, in despair of what is to come, have destroyed our life in beastlike pleasures.
One fish [?] with what is useful. And what will you say, you who live in idleness? And idleness is the beginning of passion.
And let no one plead ignorance as an excuse, for a natural reason has been planted within us,

which shows us how to shun what is harmful and to acquire what is useful. I do not depart from the examples of the sea, for these lie before us for examination. I have heard from certain seafarers that the sea urchin,
a small and contemptible creature, sometimes becomes the teacher of sailors about the calm and the stirring of the sea.
For when it perceives that a storm is going to come, it seizes a heavy stone, clings to it and does not let it move, as if in the manner of a ship's anchors, so that the waves may not carry it away.
And when the sailors see this sign, they know that violence of the wind is coming.
None of the astrologers,

nor any of the Chaldeans, who discern the turbulence [?] of the air by the rising of the stars, taught it this. Rather, the Lord of the sea and the winds has made in this small creature a clear sign of his own wisdom.
Nothing before God is contemptible and uncared for. That unsleeping eye sees all things, and everything is before him.
God, who did not leave the sea urchin to be neglected, would he neglect [your] affairs?
Husbands, love [your wives]. Your union is from places far apart, but the bond of nature and the yoke of blessing is what brings about the union of those who are distant. Of all creeping things [?],
[?] meets the sea serpent which is called the moray; it calls it from the depths for their union.
And she comes and becomes a wife to that biter.

And what then is the lesson of this? That even though he is harsh and wild of mind, it is indeed necessary for the wife to bear with him and not to break up that union on the pretext that he is a biter. But [?] he is a member. Let the husband too hear this instruction of righteousness!
If that viper casts out its venom in honor of marriage, will you not cast away the bitterness of your soul in honor of union?
And perhaps let us profit from the example of the viper in another respect as well, for that joining of the viper and the moray is fornication. And let them be instructed,
those who corrupt another's marriage, and let them know which reptile they resemble. But for me there is only one profit: that I may be of profit to the churches in every way.

Let the passion of adulterers be driven out by [the examples] of the sea! And let this discourse be halted here, of necessity, because of the weakness of the body and the coming of evening. Were it not for this, the wonder of the plants in the sea would indeed have been added,
and of the sea itself: how it congeals and becomes salt, and how coral, a precious stone, is grass in the sea, and when it is brought out into the air, it hardens to the hardness of stone;
and whence, in that feeble two-shelled creature, nature created within it a precious stone, which is the pearl of great price,

which the treasury of the king desires, and [?] among hard rocks in its shell; whence the pinna nourishes that golden wool, which none of the dyers has been able to dye to this day; and whence the snail, which is called the kochlios, their [?], whose color has surpassed the flowers of paradise?
"Let the waters bring forth." And what was not made at once, every useful thing, [?] without will? And what fruitfulness was not granted for the life of human beings?
Some were made for the service of human beings, some for making known the wonders of created things, and others to terrify our negligence.
God created, as if in kind, the great sea monsters and [?]; for this reason they were called great,
but even more because they are like great mountains, until they come to resemble great regions.
But these [?] the deep which is called the Atlantic.
These are the ones that were created to terrify and astonish us.
And when you hear about the small fish called the echeneis, which stops great ships traveling with a fair wind,
and does not let them move at all, but they stand as though fixed in the depths,
let that be a teacher to you. The sea creatures [?] and dolphins and those like them are only terrifying, but also that thorn of the Egyptian sea [?],
when it dies. And again the hare: they are not only terrifying, but they swiftly bring about destruction.
And your Creator wills it so, in order that you may be watchful and, through hope in him, flee from those harmful things.
But let us come up from the depths to the land.
For the wonders of created things have poured over us as waves, and they have drawn out our words like wounds [?]. And it is no wonder if, when our minds see the many wonders of the dry land,
it should again flee back to the sea, like Jonah.

And it seems to me that this discourse of mine has forgotten measure because of the multitude of wonders, and that there has happened to it what happens to those who travel by sea, who do not perceive their progress because of the speed of their running. So, through the course of the discourse about created things, we have not sensed the length of the discourse. That which is desired [?] is loving of hearing,
and the voice of the Lord is sweet to hearers in the narration of great wonders. But let us halt this discourse just here, and wait for the day to deliver what remains.
And let us all rise and give thanks for what has been said and for what remains.
And let it be for us, when we take food at table, that we remember the things narrated; let them be spoken of in the morning and the evening,
so that we may remember them even in sleep, to say:
"I sleep, but my heart is awake." [His] is the glory and the might to the ages of ages, amen.
Discourse of Saint Basil, chapter eight. "And God said: Let the earth bring forth living, ensouled creatures, each according to its kind, four-footed animals and creeping things!
and beasts. And it was so." The earth too [?] its own adornment.
"And let the waters bring forth creeping things having breath" ... "let the earth bring forth a living soul." Is the earth then alive with a soul? And they may find [reason to say] that
"the earth is alive with a soul." But it is not so, as was said: "Let the earth bring forth." By this it brought forth whatever was in it:
rather, the one who gave the command gave it the power to bring forth.
And it is not that "Let the earth bring forth green grass and fruit-bearing tree" means that a hidden seed was already in it and that it then brought this forth,
nor that it made palms and oaks sprout in this way; rather, the divine word is the nature of beings. "Let the earth bring forth":
not what was in it, for God gives it the power of coming into being.
And likewise here too, "Let the earth bring forth a soul" does not mean a soul lying in it,
but the one given to it by the command of God. And so their argument is refuted once more.
For if the earth brought forth its own soul, is it then itself left soulless? But their abominable error is made known by this.
Why were the waters commanded to bring forth creeping things, living souls, and the earth a living soul?
And we suppose that the nature of swimming creatures has an imperfect nature, because their existence comes from the thickness of the water.
For this reason they are heavy of hearing and sluggish, for they see [?]; and they have neither memory, nor imagination, nor knowledge of what is their own.
For this reason the saying indicated, as it were, that bodily life came first; [?] has perfect life, and for this reason governance was commanded to them first.

For their senses are more [?] (sharpened?), their grasp of what lies before them is swift, and memory of things past is present in most of them. That is why ensouled bodies were created for the water.
For from the waters were created creeping things, ensouled living creatures, but of the dry land, of bodies [?].
It is as though those that live on the earth are greater in living power. Those of the dry land are irrational beasts,
but each of them by its own voice signifies by nature many affections of its own self,
such as grief, and recognition of its companions, and lack of food, and the loss of its companions.
And they signify manifold affections by their voice. But those of the water not only have no voice, but they are also [?] and untaught, and they are of no use for sharing in human life.
"The ox knew its manger and the ass its owner." The fish does not know the one who feeds it.

The ass recognizes the voice to which it is accustomed; [?] its own [?]; it is keener than all in hearing [?]. [?] do not have such remembrance of wrongs, but it remembers a wrong for a long time, and when it finds an opportune place, it repays it with evil.
Listen, you resentful ones, who practice evil as though it were virtue:

you who, like that animal, like a spark in ashes, find some pretext and then kindle your [?] like a fire. "Let the earth bring forth a living soul." Why did he speak of the soul in connection with the earth? So that you may know the difference between the soul of the beast and the soul of man. And a little later you will learn how the soul of man was made.
And now, as for the soul of the animal: for it is written that the soul of every animal is blood. When blood congeals,
it becomes flesh, and when flesh decays,

it returns to earth. Therefore it is a breathing creature: "Let the earth bring forth a breathing creature." See the sequence of the breathing creature: blood becomes flesh and flesh becomes earth. And again, undoing it, he turned it back from earth into flesh, from flesh into blood, and from blood into a breathing creature. Do not think
that their souls existed before their bodies came into being, or that they remain [?] after their flesh dissolves.
Flee from the vain talk of the arrogant philosophers, who are [not?] ashamed to hold that their soul and the soul of dogs are one,
who say that they themselves were once plants and fish of the sea. Those who write this are [like?] fish [?].
"Let the earth bring forth a breathing creature." Perhaps many are surprised that I suddenly fell silent for a long time after the running course of my words.
Yet to the more understanding among the hearers the reason for this would not seem unknown,

how could it not have occurred [?]: you look at one another, and with signs of the eye you direct me: "See, many of the creatures, and no small ones, we have forgotten, and almost [?] in the discourse [?]."
"Let them bring forth living creatures, kind by kind, and winged birds upon the earth, upon the firmament" — concerning the swimming creatures,
as much as [?], and [we turned] to the investigation of the creatures of the dry land, and in this we forgot the birds.
And it happens to us as it happens to travelers: when they have forgotten something they need, even though they have gone very far, they nevertheless turn back,
so that they may incur toil as the fitting penalty for losing it. So it is right for us also to turn back, for what was left out is not small,
but a third part of the creation of living things, for the kinds of living things are three: those of the earth, those of the waters, and those of the air.

"Let the waters bring forth creeping breathing creatures, living things kind by kind, and winged birds upon the earth, which fly in the firmament of heaven, kind by kind." Why the creation of birds [?], and the kinship between birds and swimming creatures: the fish cleaves the water and goes forward by the movement of its fins, and by the movement of its tail it steers its course in whatever direction it wishes,
and in the same way we see the bird as it swims in the air with its wings.
And inasmuch as this [?] of theirs is one, yet,
there is none [?]; all of them are from the earth [?], and therefore of necessity they need feet. But to those other birds feet were given for their service and for procuring their food.
And some birds are poor in feet,

and their feet are not useful for walking or [?]. Examples are the swallow and the swift, which catch their food from the creatures that live in the air. To the swallow, flight close to the ground has been given in place of feet.
And if many were to investigate, as we investigated concerning the class of fish,
they would find many distinctions among birds, in their sizes, and shapes, and colors, and ways of life,
and activities; and you would find it necessary [?] that they should give them names. And they marked out the particular character of each kind.
Some they have called split-winged, for example the eagle; others the bat;
others the wasp; and others are in a sheath [?] when they emerge from that sheath. But for us, what many have said about the knowledge of fishes is enough,

And those that the book of the saints set apart, the carnivorous ones: their constitution is different and suited to the management of their way of life — the sharpness of their claws and the curve of their beak.
and the swiftness of their wings, so that they may quickly seize prey and eat it.
And the form of seed-eaters is different, and the form of those that graze is different [?].
Some flock together, apart from the predatory ones only, for there is none among these that would associate with another, except only in mating [?].
And there are also many others that love to live in great numbers, such as doves, cranes [?], starlings [?] and partridges.
And again, among these there are some that have no leader, and there are some among them that submit to a leader, as, for example, the cranes [?].

And there is a difference among them, for some of them do not move from their own land, and some of them travel far away. And when winter approaches, most birds depart to foreign parts. [?] are raised at home by them, and because of [?] they cannot bear the handling of human hands.
And some live alongside humans, and others are solitary, lovers of the wilderness. They have great variety in the distinctive character of their voices.
Some are talkative, and some are silent.
And some are merry [?] neither merriment nor song. And some are imitators [?], either by their own nature or [?]; and some have a voice that does not change.
The cock is proud, the peacock loves beauty, the dove loves lechery, and the domestic hen likewise is always lustful.
The partridge is cunning and jealous, and in its malice it helps hunters in their hunting.
And their activities and ways of life differ in many ways, as we have said.
Some are civic creatures, for the intent of each one of them is, through its activity, the benefit of all [?], as we see in the bee.
For their dwelling is one,
and their flight is of one kind, and their work is one and the same. They [?] their work at the command of the king, and they cannot fly out to the garden until he himself has flown up.

And they do not have a king who has been elected (and sometimes an evil king is elected through the rash choice of the people), nor is their rule obtained by lot, for rule by lot [?] thereby the rule of the worst of the people,
nor is their rule hereditary, for such rulers have neither education nor knowledge, and sometimes they are devoid of all virtue because of their pampering and luxury.
But the king of the bees has rule over all by nature, for he surpasses them all in body and form and in gentleness of soul.
And that king of theirs has no sting [?] takes vengeance, like a tormentor [?].
And those who [?] the likeness of their king, by the striking of their own sting it dies.
Hear, Christians, you who are commanded not to repay anyone evil for evil, but to overcome evil with good: imitate the character of the bee,
for it spoils nothing belonging to anyone, nor does it harm anyone else's fruit, and it builds its own house.
And it gathers wax from flowers and honey from the dews that are among those flowers.
And it takes it up in its mouth and brings it to the wax cell. For this reason it is at first [?] it comes to its proper measure and sweetness.

For this reason it has received in the Proverbs the good praises that befit it, and it has been called a wise worker and a gatherer of its food, from which kings and people of every age [?] with wisdom the treasuries of honey!
And from the wax it spreads a thin skin and builds the cells pressed against one another, so that their pressing against one another may be a bond and a strength for all.
For each of its cells is separated from the others by its wax crust, and again in one place they are two-storied and sometimes three-storied;
and they take care that one cell not inflict its moisture on another and the honey run out. Consider that work [?] of the earth [?], and see those six-cornered cells of wax,
It does not [?], so that their bases may not be weakened, but the walls below [support] the upper part, and each one [has] its moisture [?].
How shall I tell you everything truly about the birds and about each one? They take turns [?]; some of them sleep,
and some stand around them and guard them while they sleep. And when one watch has passed, [the bird on watch] cries out and goes to sleep,

and a second one relieves it, and it takes its turn at keeping watch [?]. For they take turns in leading: one flies in front for some time, and then turns back to the rear, and the leading passes to another. And the race of storks is not far from the understanding of rational beings.
For they come to these parts at one time, and all at once [?] them; and it seems to me that they [?] them.
And the sign of this is the following: when the storks depart, no crow at all is to be found here, and again,
for after this they return wounded and show marks. [?] Did someone lay down for the crows the law of love for strangers? From whom did they fear the infliction of punishment,
were it not that they were being pressed [?] by those of theirs [?] who shut their doors and do not let strangers in at night!
And that labor which [?] for their sake of their parents [?].
And no one is so lacking in understanding that he would be inferior in virtue to the irrational birds.
And when a stork becomes [?] with old age, its young surround it and warm it with their wings.
And they bring it food without fail, so that it may grow strong enough to fly;
then little by little they lift its wings and make it fly, so that it may feed along with them.

And this [?] for all [?] the repayment of good [is called?] 'stork-like repayment.' Let no one lament because of poverty, nor over his life, when there is no money in his house, but let him look to the resourcefulness of the swallow. For she, when she fastens together her nest, carries straw in her mouth, and as much [?] with her foot [?], but she wets her wings with water and then [?] them, she seeks out clay for it, to use for joining it together, one piece to another, with that clay as with glue, and she raises her young in it.

And if someone puts out the eyes of her young, by that [?] she restores the eyes of her young to health again. These teach you not to do evil because of poverty, and not [?] all that is yours, and not to remain [?] and idle,
but to flee to God; for God, if such a means [?] those who entreat him with all their heart [?]!
The halcyon is a sea bird. And it makes a nest for its young by the shore, in the middle of [?], when the winds are fierce and the sea casts up onto the land.
But during those seven days the wind and the sea grow calm, and on the seventh day it hatches its young.
And God grants this small creature another seven calm days for feeding its young:
so that even all sailors know these halcyon [days] in every [?],
in which your deliverance may come from God's care for you,
What sort of image are you, this stilling of the great sea for the sake of a small [?]?
They say that the turtledove, once she has been parted from her mate, no longer joins with another, because of that first union.

Hear this, women, how this beauty of widowhood [surpasses?] much marrying. And one of them it throws down to the ground with its wing, and the other it rears. The first, because of the labor of feeding.
But they say that another bird, which is called the phene, does not let that chick of hers die, [rearing it?] together with its own.
So too are those parents who cast out their children on the pretext of poverty,
and those who do not treat their children equally in the division of the inheritance.
And thus it is right that, just as they were the cause of their being, so also they should give all of them equally the means of their living.
Do not imitate, O man, the hardheartedness of certain birds, whose chicks, when they are fledged and flying,
they peck at and chase with their wings, until they drive them out to fend for themselves [?].
For how greatly it follows after them, even when they are flying, and feeds them for a long time!
And many birds have no need of union with a male in order to give birth; and there are others that have no seed, and they are facing the wind [?].
And they say that the vulture for the most part gives birth without a male, and that it is long-lived, for at times it lives [?]. For the sake of the mention of birds: when you see someone
who laughs at our mystery and says, "This is outside of nature, and it cannot be

that a virgin should give birth and her virginity remain still undefiled": for he whom it pleased to bring salvation to those who believe in him through that preaching of foolishness also did many wonders in nature for the confirmation of faith.
Let the waters bring forth creeping things, living souls, and winged birds upon the earth, which fly in the firmament of heaven.
It was commanded that they should fly above the earth,

for the food of all of them is upon the earth. We said earlier that 'heaven' was the name given to the place that appears [?], and he called it 'firmament' because of its density, from the vapours that rise up. And you have the heaven adorned, the sea fruitful with its offspring,
and the air full of birds.

that fly in it, which came into being by the command of God. And now, all that the discourse has cut short out of caution against much speaking, you who are wakeful by nature, consider it without ceasing and glorify the Creator from his creatures!
And let you have at night the multitude of the birds of the night, and by day those of the day.

Bats and owls and night-crows, so that when you are awake you may reflect on them; let these be enough for you, so that you may fully investigate the particular nature of each. There is the swallow-[?] bird, which, when it sits on its eggs, does not cease crying out all night long! And how the bat is winged and four-footed, and of all of them it alone has teeth, and it lives like a four-footed animal,
and it flies in the air not with a feathered wing but with a membrane of skin.
And how they are together with one another, which is not easy for people to do; such a thing is only far removed from theirs [?].

Those who have given their leisure to vain philosophy. For the eyes of the owl are sound at night, but when the sun [?]; so their minds are [?] in vanity, but for seeing the true light they are darkened.
And again, the wonders of the Creator by day, from many [creatures].

How that bird that lives with you rouses you to work with its piercing voice! It cries out and from afar announces the rising of the sun, and early at dawn it gets travelers up and sends farmers out to reap. How wakeful is the race of geese, and how keen of sense regarding those who steal away [?]!

By them the royal city of Rome was once saved, when men of war came against it and dug tunnels under the ground, and little remained and part of Rome [?], until they cackled [?] and made the deed of those men known.
And does the vulture not have some particular property [concerning] the death of men, before it comes to pass, when they are arrayed against one another?
And see the great flock of vultures, when they follow a battle camp and learn what is to come from the preparation of the men's weapons.
And this is not far from human reasoning.
How shall I tell you of the multitude of locusts, which, when they encamp together and arrive at some field, do not approach the crop until they receive a command

from God? And how the bird called the seleucis pursues them, as a cure for the plague of locusts, with an untold capacity for eating; for the merciful God created its nature greedy for the benefit of humankind.
What is the delight of the cicada? And how is its voice at its highest at midday, when it breathes in the hot air and sends forth that chirping from its chest?

But I think that I have dwelt [?] too long on the birds. And if it were possible to reach [?] — when I saw the segmented winged creatures, that is, the bee and the wasp, for they are called so because of this — consider their breathing [?], not from all their members [?]. Therefore,
when they are smeared with oil they die, because the pores of their bodies are blocked; and if vinegar is sprinkled on them at once, they come back to life, because their pores open again.

And nothing is lacking. Again, when you look at the water-loving creeping creatures, you will find great variety among them: they do not have split feet like the crow's, nor curved ones like those of the carnivorous birds.
Rather, their feet are flat and like skin, so that it may be easy for them; they push the water aside as if with oars.
And when you observe the heron, as it plunges its neck into the depths and draws up its food from there, then you will find the wisdom of the Creator,
for this is why he made its neck longer than its feet,
so that it may snatch up the food hidden below as if with tongs. For the word of Scripture, when someone reads it, is like a trickle [?]: 'Let the waters bring forth feathered flying creatures
that fly over the earth and the firmament of heaven.' And when the sense of the word is carefully examined, then the greatness of the wonders of the Creator's wisdom appears.
How many birds there are! How he distinguished them, how he adorned each of them with the distinctive character of each kind: this day will fail me in telling you of the wonders of the air.
The earth summons us to show forth the beasts and the reptiles and the grazing animals, ready to make known to us what corresponds to the plants and to the race of swimming creatures and birds.
Let the earth bring forth the living soul of cattle and of beasts and of reptiles, each according to its kind.

What do you say, you who deny the resurrection, when you see the transformation of many living creatures of the air? As they report to us about the worm of India, which has horns, which is at first a worm and stays in that form, but then it flies with wings, broad ones. O women, when you sit down to wash [?] your spun thread, which the silkworm makes for you for the hem [?] of soft clothing,
remember the transformation of that living creature, and gain a true understanding of the transformation of the resurrection, and believe in that transformation
of which Paul spoke. But I think that this discourse has gone beyond its proper measure.
When I looked, I considered myself to be beyond measure. And again, when I looked, I thought that I had not yet even begun my telling.
And can this lingering be done? For no hosts inviting you to a meal are hurrying you, and no fellow guests [?] are waiting for you,
but spiritually, for the souls of bodies [?], delight in the Lord, and he will give you what is in your heart. You are a lover of wealth:
You have spiritual wealth: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous;

with it they are more to be desired than gold and much precious carbuncle. You are delighted and full of longing; you have the words of God, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. If I dismiss this assembly, some of them will go off to the table with an evil intent [?], with the sickness of greed.

For the devil runs between those two speckled bones, kindling this frenzy, and he overturns the vessels and makes the one glad with the victory and the other sorrowful, and again the one becomes cheerful and the other ashamed.
What benefit is the fasting of the body, when the soul is filled with evil?
As for the one who does not play at the gaming table but is at leisure for something else, what vain thing will he not say? What worse thing will he not hear? For leisure,
which is without anything whatever [?], is also [?]. But even this lingering and my being with you is also a restraint from evil.

And this statement is sufficient before a prudent judge, if someone does not hope for a reward for what is vain, but considers the weakness of our strength and the measure of the delight of those standing here.
The earth has come to meet you with its plants, the sea with fish, the air with birds. And again the earth.
It has been prepared, so that he may show you what follows upon this, so that the evening food may not weary you through excessive satiety. But he who has filled all things with his own,
he, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might unto the ages. Lines (stichoi): 590 [?].
Discourse of Saint Basil, chapter nine. How did that table of today's words seem to you?
But I, who wish that I might be [like] one of the rich who honor [their guests],

who, when the bread set out as food has dried up for lack of relish, sets the humble food on the table generously, so that by it he greatly rebukes this greatly [?], although you say something otherwise, but as the case is. You were not bold before his friends [?], although he spread out [?] wild herbs. Understand the change of words, not of my own saying but as said by another,
those who [do not take Scripture] in the common [sense] [?] and do not say that water is water,
but say that it is some other nature, and interpret fish in whatever way they please;

and again they interpret the nature of reptiles and wild beasts according to their own designs, like interpreters of dreams, at their own will. But I, when I hear 'grass', understand grass; and a plant, [and] a fish [?], I understand [as such].
Nor am I ashamed of our Gospel. [?] of the earth, that it has the shape of a ball, or else the shape of a [?], round on every side,

like something rubbed smooth, or else deep and round in its middle; and those who wrote about the world arrived at such a consideration. And each of them refutes what his fellow has said. Not that I think on this account that this statement of ours about the world would be blameworthy, since Moses, the servant of God, did not speak about the shapes of the earth, nor did he say

that the extent of the earth is twelve myriads of stadia, nor did he measure how much air the shadow of the earth holds at the time of the sun's coming, [?] the moon approaches the shadow of the earth, it wanes.
And however much he kept silent about what was of no use to us, are the [?] of the Holy Spirit lighter than the wisdom of those who have gone mad?
But we give thanks to him who did not make our mind preoccupied, [?] so that this might be written for our mind and for the light of our souls.

And I think that some people did not know this, and they took it to heart; it is as though someone made himself wiser than the words of the Holy Spirit and, on the pretext of interpretation, brought in his own view.

They recognize [?]: "Let the earth bring forth the living soul of cattle and beasts and reptiles." Understand God's [?] running among created things: it began then, and until now it remains active, and it hastens on to when the world is brought to its end.
And just as with a ball, when someone strikes it on a sloping place, by its roundness [?] and by the slope of the place, until [?] of what is not, by one command they were moved to being,

and to corruption they go forth evenly following their kinds, and they are to preserve their likeness, until in place of a horse [?], and a lion in place of a lion, and an eagle in place of an eagle, it preserves them one after another until the end of all things.
And nothing of time destroys the particular nature of living things, but they run on through the ages as though they were something new, as if they had only just now come into being.
"Let the earth bring forth the living soul." This command remained upon the earth, and unceasingly it [?] the Creator,

for some of them come into being by succession, and some even until now [?]; for not only cicadas, and not only the many kinds that fly in the air, which cannot be given names because of their smallness,
But the mouse and the frog also come from it: when heavy rain falls in the hot season, the fields are immediately filled with field mice. And the eel, too, comes out only from mud,

Its succession is neither from an egg nor from a cause [?]; rather, its being is from the earth. 'Let the earth bring forth living souls.' The beasts are from the earth and [return] to the earth. And just as great a difference was made between the image of creation
and its flesh, so there is a great difference of dignity between the soul of men and the soul of four-footed beasts.
And what is the form of the four-footed animals? Their head is bent down toward the earth, and it looks about and seeks pleasures in every direction.
But your head is raised toward heaven, and your eyes look upward.
And if you ever dishonor yourself through the passions of the flesh and serve the belly and what lies below the belly, you have become like the senseless beasts. The care that is fitting for you
is that you seek the things above, where your [?] above the earth. Just as the image of your creation was stamped upon you, so shape your life.

Let your citizenship be in heaven and your dwelling place the heavenly Jerusalem, and let your fellow citizens and kin be those firstborn of heaven. And the souls of beasts did not lie in the earth and only afterward appear,
but at the command [?]. And the soul of beasts is one and the same: beastly.
And each of the animals has its own many kinds of characteristics.
The ox is patiently enduring, the ass slow, the horse burning with desire for the female, the wolf untamable,
the fox crafty, the deer timid, the ant industrious, the dog grateful and mindful of affection.
As soon as each of them was created, it at once received the characteristic of its nature.
With the lion were born wrath, a solitary life, and no fellowship with its own kind. It is ruler over the beasts, and in its nature it is not content to be like the many.
And not even if it should come upon the leftovers of its own prey [?].
Nature has given it such an organ of voice that many of the animals,
