which are swifter than it, [are caught] by its own [?] alone. [?] For moisture is mingled with lightness in its body, and it follows the movements of its soul. The bear is heavy by nature and solitary [?],
and its body is heavy, chilled, and immovable.
If we follow what has been said, we shall see in these beasts much natural striving for their life, without teaching;
And this, or [?] for your great vigilance and our life, more unfailing than the beasts [?]. The bear,
when it is severely wounded, heals itself with a herb called phlomos, for its nature is dry; it stuffs its wound with it and is healed.
And the fox heals itself with pine resin.

And the tortoise, when it has gorged itself on the flesh of the viper, eats wild savory and is saved from the harm of the poison. And serpents heal their blindness when [?]. And the foreknowledge of animals concerning changes of the weather, how is it not beyond [?], since the sheep, when winter approaches, eats much, as though laying in provision against the expected want?
And the ox, when it lies down in the wintertime, lingers lying there, looking out from the stable toward the field, and it wants to go outside.

And a certain investigator observed that the land hedgehog makes two doors to its hole, and when the north wind blows, it closes the hole on the north side, and when the wind from the south side blows, it closes that one. And what does it show people by this?
Not only the care of God, which is among all things, but also that even irrational animals have a perception of what is to come,

So that we too may not look only to what lies before us, but that our zeal may be for what is our own. O man, will you not store up beforehand, in this time, the eternal rest? Look at the work of the ant: it stores up for itself in summer the food for winter. And does it let the time of gathering pass by [?]?
Rather, it hurries itself to the work until it has gathered for itself, and this not with negligence but with a wise contrivance, so that its food may last for a long time.
And this it does: for it cuts the grain apart, otherwise its food would spoil.
And it perceives when its store has been wetted by snow, and it dries it, yet not merely for the sake of drying, but when it recognizes the clearness of the air.
And no one among people sees rain pouring down from the clouds at the time when the ant is drying its food.
What word can reach this? Or what ear can contain it? Or what time would suffice,
in which we might speak and declare the wonders of the Creator?! Let us too say with the prophet: For great are your works,

O Lord, and you have made all things in wisdom. Now therefore it is not enough to justify us that we have not learned what is profitable for us from the book, since we have come to know the profit of the good by the law of nature, without teaching. Do you know how to do good to your neighbor?
For you want it to be done to you; for that is it [?], which you do not want to be done to you by another. From the making [?] of herbs,

And not by investigation of roots [?], but each [according to] its own, and the natural movement is beyond telling. And in us too there are virtues by nature, for the movement of the soul is not from the teaching of men. Just as no word teaches us to hate pain, but there is something [in us] that reminds us [?],
so too there is in the soul an avoidance of evil without teaching.

And every evil is your [? perhaps: a disease] of the soul, and the definition of virtue is the life of the soul. Some have well defined life as being the stability of the natural activities of the soul. You will not stray from what is fitting. The soul has set its heart on this,
which is in its nature without teaching.
Therefore holiness is praised before all, and justice is accepted,
and courage is admired and wisdom is loved, which are [?] beyond those of the flesh. Let children love their own fathers and mothers;
and parents, do not be angry with them. Does nature perhaps not say this very thing? Rather, it strengthens the bonds of nature.
the lioness loves her own cubs; the wolf fights for its young. What shall a man say, when he has become disobedient to nature [?],
when a son despises the old age of his father, or when a father through a second marriage forgets those first children of his?
[?] as many [?] of parents toward their own children, for God the Creator has made up for what they lack and has greatly consoled them through their senses.
Thus, among a multitude of sheep, when a lamb leaps out of the flock, it recognizes its mother's voice and, [?], leaves behind the other udders, though they are full of butter.
And likewise the lamb's mother recognizes its voice among many lambs. The color of them all [?] to our sense of smell [?],

but they have a sense sharper than ours, by which each of them recognizes what is its own. The dog wishes with its mouth to take revenge on those who harm it. The calf's horns have not yet come up, and yet they know where their weapon is to emerge. And this teaches us
that all these instincts are untaught, and that nothing among beings is worthless or undefined, but all bear a sign of the wisdom of the Creator.
And they show in themselves
that they were created ready to guard their own safety. The dog is without reason, but it has a sense that matches the power of reason.
For what the wise of the earth find only with difficulty, with all their great leisure (I mean by composition [?]), the dog [does], taught by its own nature.
For it seeks the track of the wild beast, and when it finds its track, with much [?] of deliberation [it reasons]: the beast has gone this way, or that way, or off in this direction,
or else neither that way nor this way [?] of the dogs; and then, as if it were saying, "Let us search out some other direction as well,"
and so by eliminating those false tracks. And what more than this do those do who write on the ground and reject the two propositions set before them, and [find] what is right in the third?

Moreover, the gratitude of that animal puts to shame those who are ungrateful to their benefactors. Many dogs are remembered to have died in the desert over their slain masters. Again, many dogs have become informers against murderers and have handed over the robbers

to punishment. [?] God their Creator [?] those who speak about God without judgment [?] of theirs, and at the very meal take upon themselves blasphemy against their Giver. But let us return again [?] to that which is born in great numbers.
For this reason hares bear many young, and wild goats and wild sheep give birth [?] by those flesh-eaters of theirs.

for with difficulty a lion cub tears open the womb, and so comes out, as they say. And likewise the asp eats [?] comes out and repays the mother [?] ... of beings [?] is learned without toil. Why is this animal so great and tall to look upon among the beasts? And it needs this for the following reason: if [its neck] were in proportion to its legs, it could in no way have been held up, because of its weight; and so that trunk of its serves the need of its neck.
And by it, it takes in its food and its drink.
And its legs are like pillars, without joints. If those legs of its were soft and supple,
it would be stumbling constantly and could not bear the weight.

But it does not have [?], for they could not bear the bulk of its flesh; for a knee is round and slippery and loose and trembling. For this reason that long trunk was necessary for it, to match the measure of its legs.
Do you not see towers [?], hills of flesh? Terrible is their [?]; and if those legs were spread apart and did not fit its flesh,
that animal would not have lived, except only for a little while.
But they say that it lives thirty years; those legs of its are firm and kneeless.
And its trunk, as I said, draws its food up from below; and that trunk is in form like a serpent, soft by nature.
Now therefore that saying is true which says: Nothing superfluous or deficient is found among created things.
And this animal, which is so great, God has given to us, so that it is trained and understands and is beaten,

and it endures this and teaches us truly that he has subjected all things under our feet, for he created us in his own image. And it is not only from the great animals that we ought to marvel at the wisdom of the Creator,
but from the small ones also let us gather a wonder no less than that,
just as with [?] those whose peaks, by their nearness to the clouds, always keep winter, but also with the deep valleys, which are windless and warm.
So also in the creation of animals I marvel not only at the size of the elephant, but also at the mouse itself, which is terrifying to the elephant,
and at the fineness of the scorpion's sting, how he hollowed it out like a pipe, so that from there it may pour its venom upon those it has bitten.
And let no one accuse the Creator on this account, saying that he made animals that are deadly and destructive and hostile to our life.
And if you do not accuse the one who instructs and governs and through beating purifies the unworthy [?]. The beasts exist for the testing of faith.
If you have faith in the Lord, you will trample on the asp and the viper; you will trample the lion and the dragon by faith, so that you may trample serpents and scorpions.
Did you not see Paul, when he was gathering wood, that a viper fastened on him, and how it could do him no harm, because that holy man was full of faith? You are [?]

that it has long been asked of me that I should speak [?]. I hear [?], for the hearts of the hearers accuse and cry out: what is ours we have learned [?] it is for that [?], but our own selves we do not know; and [?] the fear that is among us is to be cast out by us. Truly it resembles [?]
that the knowledge of oneself is harder than anything.
For not only does the eye see and yet not see itself, but our mind too sees the sin of another and [?] of its own.
Therefore now too the one spoken of [?] has hurried quickly on to other things, while he himself is slow and full of sluggishness [?] in examining himself; and not from heaven, nor only [from it],
but also from our own constitution let him come to know himself, as the prophet says: "Your knowledge has become wonderful from us," that is, the knowledge of your wisdom.
And God said: "Let us make man." [Where is] the Jew [?],
the one who denied, on account of the face that appeared, as an image, through the windows of light by the divine word, and was no longer himself [?]?
"And he spoke and he made." He said: "Let there be light," and there was light. Even then the refutation of their argument lay ready at hand.
What smith, or what carpenter, or what shoemaker, sitting alone at the tools of his craft with no one else working with him, would say to himself:
"Let us make a knife," or "Let us assemble a plow," or "Let us stitch shoes [?]"?
And would he not rather carry out the necessary work without speech and with a drawing of breath [?], since as ruler and master he urges himself on by command?
But those who did not know God, what indeed would they not say, since they have tongues bared for lying?
But this statement lying before us silences them: "And God said: Let us make man." Tell me now, is there one Person here?
For it was not written, "Let there be man," but "Let us make man." When there was as yet no learner, the word concerning the Godhead was in hidden depth.
And when the hope of man's existence came about, faith was made manifest and the true counsel shone forth: "Let us make man."

Do you not hear, you fighter against Christ, that he speaks to the one who is co-creator with him, through whom with him he created the ages, who bears all things by the power of his word? But he does not accept the words of faith in quietness, so that into the snare [?],
he struggles against the snares and displays [?] of his own nature, but he is not able to escape;
so too the enemies of the truth, the race of the Jews, when they are hard pressed, say that there are many persons to whom the word of God was addressed.
And when he said, "Let us make man," they say, he said it to the angels. This is a Jewish fabrication;

these are the notions of their vanity. They bring in myriads, they deny the Son, and they ascribe the honor of the Lord's counsel to servants; and those who are fellow servants with us they make lords of our creation.
Man, when he is made perfect, attains the rank of the angels.
What creature is able to attain [?]? See the words that follow: "Let us make man in our image," it says. What does he say to this? Is the image of God and of the angels one, perhaps?
But the image of the Father and of the Son is one, beyond all dispute, understood as that by which it resembles the Godhead, not by a bodily form but by the properties of the Godhead.
Listen, you too, you who are one of the innovators, who magnify Judaism under the guise of Christianity. To whom does he say, "in our likeness"? To whom else but to him
who is the radiance of glory and the image of his person, who is the image of the invisible God? [?] "man in our image," it says,
to his own living image, who said: "I and the Father are one," and:
"Whoever has seen me has seen my Father." There, "And God made man," not "they made" [?]; here the word avoids a plurality of persons.

And by this he instructs you; by this it was written against the pagans [?]. Understand the Son together with the Father, and be saved from the perdition of many gods. "In the image of God he made": he did not say "in his image," but "in the image of God."
And let us speak further on in what is to come about how man is in the image of God and how he becomes in his likeness.
But now it is said: if the image is one, from where have you arrived at this intolerable impiety, so as to say that the Son is unlike the Father?
O ingratitude toward the likeness! That of which you were made worthy, you do not grant to him!
And you suppose that the grace given to you abides with you, yet you do not confess that the Son has the likeness of the Father by nature!
But the evening commands us to fall silent, since it has sent the sun away toward the west!
And here let us stop this our discourse, so that the inquiry concerning this [?] by the holy [?].
Go with joy to the church, you lovers of Christ, and adorn those salt-seasoned tables of yours with that remembrance and with many foods.

Let the Arians be ashamed, let the Jews be turned back, and let the believer rejoice in the true answer. And let him glorify [?] and the power unto the ages of ages; amen. Glory to God, the accomplisher of all good.
